#4365. Invictus Gaming beat Top Esports 3-1 to reach first Worlds semi-final since 2019

Invictus Gaming knocked out fellow LPL side Top Esports in the opening quarter-final of Worlds 2026 in Allen, Texas. The result guarantees China a semi-final place after the LPL's 0-4 start in the Swiss Stage.

Invictus Gaming are through to the last four of Worlds 2026. They beat fellow LPL side Top Esports in the opening match of the Knockout Stage. The series was played at the Credit Union of Texas Event Center in Allen, Texas, on 3 November (US time).

The win guarantees China a semi-final place. That matters after the LPL’s 0-4 start in the Swiss Stage. IG now meet either Gen.G or LYON. Gen.G beat IG 1-0 in the Swiss Stage and finished it with a perfect 3-0 record.

TES played the event without ZUIAN. On 6 October the club announced that Bai ‘369’ Jia-Hao would move into the starting line-up because of visa problems affecting ZUIAN.

The stand-in still made his mark. IG won Game 1 after building a gold lead of more than 10,000. TES levelled in Game 2 when 369, on Renekton, killed JiaQi and TheShy on his own late in the game. IG then took the next two games to close out the series.

Every Knockout Stage match is a single-elimination best-of-five played with Fearless Draft. The two sides knew each other well. They met twice in best-of-five series in September. IG won 3-2 in the LPL Split 3 playoffs on 5 September. TES won 3-1 in the LPL Regional Finals on 17 September.

The prize money gap is now fixed. Worlds 2026 has a total prize pool of US$5,000,000, with US$1,000,000 for the winner. Each losing semi-finalist receives US$400,000, so IG are guaranteed at least that sum.

IG’s run began with a mid-season rescue. The team started LPL Split 3 in the Nirvana Group. The club then asked TheShy and Rookie, who were both on a break, to come back. The pair helped the side qualify for Worlds. Both won the 2018 world title with IG.

TheShy said he had promised IG’s CEO he would help if asked. “I came back to keep my word,” he said after the series.

The #Worlds2026 Knockout Stage bracket after today's match! pic.twitter.com/iaPQndNZSW

— LoL Esports (@lolesports) November 4, 2026

The rest of the quarter-finals follow this week. Gen.G play LYON on 4 November. Dplus KIA face Bilibili Gaming on 5 November. Europe’s last team, Karmine Corp, play T1 on 6 November. All three start at 16:00 CT.

The semi-finals will be played in Allen on 7 and 8 November. The final will be held in Brooklyn on Saturday 14 November at 2pm EST.

#4364. Google Adds Ocarina of Time Easter Egg Ahead of Remake Release

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

The original version of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time launched in November of 1998, which was a positively jam-packed year for gaming. Coincidentally, that was around the time that Google first launched, introducing the world to the wonders of online searching and taking its first step to becoming an ever-ubiquitous behemoth.

Nintendo's storefronts in New York City and San Francisco will be holding reservation-only midnight launches, with registration opening later today.

Because of this link, not to mention Google and Ocarina of Time’s respective vital places in the history of pop culture, it’s not unreasonable for one to give some flowers to the other, particularly on the precipice of a major revival.

In case you somehow managed to forget, this Thursday, November 5, the full remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will be launching for the Nintendo Switch 2, a graphical and gameplay overhaul of one of Nintendo’s most beloved games of all time. In recognition of this event, Google has added a new easter egg to its sizable catalog of hidden tricks and silly sight gags. All you have to do to trigger it is search “Zelda Ocarina of Time,” and click the little glowing sword that appears in the bottom right.

Google’s Ocarina of Time easter egg takes the form of the classic Master Sword pedestal located in the Temple of Time in the game. When you first perform the search, the Master Sword has already been removed from the pedestal, emanating an ethereal blue glow.

However, when you click the Master Sword, Link’s distinctive grunt sounds out, and the screen is engulfed in that blue glow, accompanied by a golden Triforce sigil. When the view clears, Google’s current veneer has completely disappeared, replaced instead by the much more simplistic results list Google would have displayed during its inception way back in 1998. Clicking the sword again will have Link grunt as he removes the sword from the pedestal, returning you to the normal Google search page.

Google’s Ocarina of Time easter egg takes the form of the classic Master Sword pedestal located in the Temple of Time in the game.

Obviously, this is a reference to how, in Ocarina of Time, when Link pulls the Master Sword from its pedestal, he’s placed in suspended animation and whisked into the future as an adult. Inversely, upon returning the Master Sword to its pedestal, he’s returned to the past in his youth. The only difference is that Link was only sealed for seven years, whereas it’s been nearly 30 years since Google’s advent, but y’know, details.

Google easter egg antics are well-known among frequent users (i.e. pretty much everyone), usually being added to the platform in reference to popular movies and shows, or to coincide with major holidays, pop culture phenomena, and so forth. It’s a fun little way to celebrate things that personally interest you, and in the specific case of Nintendo games, there have been a few different ones.

Searching “Pokémon” in Google brings up a little PokéBall that, when clicked, allows you to play a minigame in which you can attempt to “catch” the original 151 by searching their names based on silhouettes and basic descriptions. Searching “Splatoon” shows a small colored blotch that, when clicked, allows you to fire shots of ink all over your results page, then click the convenient button to quickly wash it off.

Google has had a particular affinity for the Mario franchise over the years. Currently, if you search “Super Mario Bros.” on Google, you’ll see a little ? Block that you can click for coins, 100 of which plays the 1-UP sound. Previously, in celebration of Mario Day 2018, Mario appeared in a kart in lieu of the Google Maps navigational arrow, with a similar coin-generating sound player also included.

Nintendo's latest trailer revealed the “Hall of Fallen Foes,” a brand-new area that allows players to revisit some boss fights.

#4363. Nintendo Switch Sports Resort Review - Still In Motion

Originating as a tech demo for the Wii’s motion controls, Nintendo’s Sports series has always found novel and intuitive ways to emulate various athletic endeavors with motion-based video game controllers. Like its predecessors, Switch Sports Resort is a compilation of sports-based minigames built around approachability. Though rightfully known for its enticing multiplayer options, Switch Sports Resort adds new single-player objectives and modes to offer a well-rounded experience for all player counts, making it perhaps the strongest entry in the series to date.

Switch Sports Resort delivers 12 main events to choose from, each with distinct controls, strategies, and rules. Mainstays like bowling, archery, boxing, and golf were my initial destinations to attempt to relive old glories, but newcomers like thumb wrestling, skateboarding, power cruising, and prop plane made me glad for their inclusion.

Skateboarding, power cruising, and prop plane form a new category called leisure sports, which allow for timed exploration of the newly renovated Wuhu Island by land, sea, and sky, respectively. I spent several sessions seeking out landmarks and collecting Spocco Points, the in-game currency used for character customization. And since all the sports’ controls are so intuitive and newcomer-friendly, it was a breeze to jump between activities.

Though they all boil down to moving your arms in something approximating motions you’d make playing the real sport, Nintendo has smartly implemented more variety in its control schemes, all while keeping them easy to pick up. Before the tutorial even explains how to hold the Joy-Con, you can likely accurately guess what the grip and motion will be; even more involved control schemes like basketball and volleyball are easy to remember.

Skateboarding is particularly innovative, as it uses Switch 2’s Joy-Con’s mouse mode to emulate the kick-push of a skater. Meanwhile, prop plane has you holding your Joy-Con like a paper airplane as you fly around blasting balloons and visiting landmarks. However, holding the Joy-Con that way for several minutes inevitably cramped my hand. And though boxing remains one of my favorite sports in the bundle, I needed to retrain my brain, as throwing a punch the correct way doesn’t work with how the game wants you to do it; if I turn my wrist when punching, my character sways instead of attacking.

Playing with friends, both online and in-person, remains the highlight of Switch Sports Resort. The online friend lobby system receives a boost in the form of allowing different sports to take place simultaneously within the same lobby, and when you add in special variants like simultaneous archery, 100-pin bowling, skateboard racing, and prop plane balloon battles, you have a lot of fun options with which to jump in.

Whenever I play solo, the Island Crown is where I spend most of my time. Here, you climb the ranks across nine sports, sometimes with special rulesets, vanquishing NPC opponents until you are the champion. Whether it was taking to increasingly outlandish bowling lanes, windier archery ranges, or simply facing off against more strategic table tennis players, I relished in improving my skills en route to the championship.

Because these minigames are relatively surface level, they have diminishing returns once you reach a certain skill level. While I loved it when my tennis opponents started challenging me to use better angles and my fellow golfers stopped air-mailing their tee shots straight into the trees, higher-skill opponents rarely energized me; instead, sports like bowling that include fun, off-the-wall variants were my favorite ladders to ascend, as they truly put my skills to the test as I was forced to adapt to moving obstacles and ramps. I just wish Nintendo injected more fun twists to keep the experiences fresh.

After completing each activity, you’re awarded Spocco Points, which you use to unlock themed customization elements for your characters. Cartoon-like Sportsmates replace the iconic Mii characters introduced in Wii Sports, but you can still use your Mii if you choose. Though I have fondness for Mii characters, after two entries featuring the more expressive, customizable Sportsmates, I now prefer those character models.

Nintendo Switch Sports Resort delivers a capable compilation of quick-hit sports minigames that can be easily enjoyed regardless of how many people are holding Joy-Cons. Though I certainly have my destination sports, there’s not a loser in the bunch. Island Crown mode does a great job expanding the single-player options, but this package’s legs are in its multiplayer experience. And since Switch Sports Resort is chock-full of easily approachable minigames, I can see it becoming a cherished inclusion in the rotation of party mainstays.

#4362. 10 RPGs That Are Unexpected Masterpieces

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

Thanks to the diversity with which the genre can be expressed, role-playing video games constitute a large part of my favorite experiences in the interactive medium, as they encompass a practically unparalleled plethora of possibilities.

Both an isometric horror title and a first-person medieval fantasy can be RPGs, giving all players, regardless of their tastes, the opportunity to find tailor-made masterpieces within the genre.

Of course, being among the most popular categories in the entire industry, finding an adventure curated to suit our tastes is no easy task, as it's common to need dozens of hours to fully enjoy each of its journeys.

Therefore, in order to save you many afternoons and with the aim of appealing to as many gaming interests as possible, I invite you to read this list of ten RPGs that are unexpected masterpieces.

If you like Paper Mario, you already know exactly what Bug Fables: The Everlasting Sapling has to offer, though I say this as one of the highest compliments I can give.

It's a game with very traditional foundations but an execution brimming with personality, offering a compelling world and story that truly keeps you engaged, especially due to its unique theme.

However, its greatest marvel lies in its gameplay. From exploration to turn-based combat combinations, side quests, bosses, and customization, the overall mechanics work flawlessly, captivating both newcomers and veterans of this type of game.

This independently created gem from Panama deserves all the recognition it can get. Rest assured, Bug Fables: The Everlasting Sapling is such an outstanding work that, at times, I think it surpasses its main inspiration.

Speaking of surpassing your muses, I've read many discussions about Path of Exile already surpassing Diablo, and frankly, comparing the most recent performance of both franchises, I find it difficult to argue otherwise.

Although they have different approaches, it's undeniable that Grinding Gear Games' creation, both the original and its sequel, has reached such levels of content density and attention to detail that they ceased to be "a clone" many years ago.

Instead, we're talking about one of the greatest representatives of the isometric RPG genre, with a consistently captivating experience that puts your job at risk because, once it hooks you, it only lets go after several hundred hours.

Imagining in 2013 that Path of Exile could go head-to-head with its category's benchmarks seemed impossible, but today, what's truly unbelievable is calling it anything less than a masterpiece of its kind.

Since the end of the last decade, efforts to find a true successor to Disco Elysium have tripled year after year, but even so, I couldn't have anticipated that a game like Esoteric Ebb would be its true spiritual heir.

Although it boasts enough distinctions to stand on its own merits, it's clear that the foundation was laid by the 2019 marvel, which allowed Christoffer Bodegård to craft an outstanding adventure from the dialogue to the worldbuilding and immersion.

Each narrative path is more captivating than the last, and even without voice acting, which forces you to read for hours on end, the cadence and rhythm between exploration and conversations, both internal and with others, are measured with truly commendable precision.

If you're a fan of Disco Elysium or Dungeons & Dragons, Esoteric Ebb strikes a perfect balance that, I can say with complete certainty, no other title this decade has even come close to achieving.

If you're looking for a 16-bit adventure, these SEGA Genesis RPGs are a great place to start.

A decade and a half ago, The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim's release sparked a subsequent odyssey to become the next great medieval first-person RPG, and I believe that title finally belongs to Tainted Grail: The Fall of Avalon.

The mere comparison is the highest honor that can be bestowed upon this wonderful dark fantasy, which nevertheless knows perfectly well how to distinguish itself from Bethesda's icy landscapes without losing an ounce of immersion.

Moreover, the title manages to compensate for its idol's weaknesses by including choices that truly feel meaningful, as well as a much more fluid and demanding combat system that not only increases the challenge but also the reward of leveling up and becoming gradually more skilled.

Considering the remarkable post-launch support that its developers provided for free, Tainted Grail: The Fall of Avalon is a blessing for the genre that deserves to be rewarded with a chance.

Dread Delusion looks further back than the 2011 Game of the Year and draws its inspiration from two superb titles, The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind and King's Field, and the result is as outstanding as you'd expect from that combination.

Its distinctive aesthetic, blending a feverish PlayStation 1 dream with a lush color palette, immediately captivates the eye, yet the experience truly enchants for hours thanks to the sheer satisfaction of getting lost in its picturesque settings.

That said, you need a very high tolerance for its combat, as it lacks depth and isn't particularly rewarding. Rather, it's a necessary sacrifice to immerse yourself in its splendid world, which is worth every second.

It's a tougher recommendation, especially in modern times, given how much better it feels when you're not using your weapons, but make no mistake: Dread Delusion is one of those titles that, if it's right for you, will win you over thoroughly.

There are certain video games whose ultimate goal is to hook you for hundreds of hours without you even realizing it or being able to stop, and Grim Dawn is undoubtedly one of them.

I went in expecting to find a good RPG and little else, and ended up finding a lifelong companion that I would spend countless afternoons with, mainly due to its absurdly deep and satisfying replayability.

The art is superb, the music is tremendous, the story and atmosphere stand out, the creativity with which it allows you to experiment with builds is impressive... It has everything you could expect from an ARPG, and even more.

For how magnificent it is, I'm afraid Grim Dawn isn't talked about enough, and precisely for this reason, you wouldn't expect that behind it lies one of the most magnificent isometric role-playing games ever made.

There are still numerous RPG gems to enjoy before the year ends.

Appearances in the video game industry are easily deceiving because the essence lies in interaction. This allows a pixel art game like Look Outside to appear harmless, while beneath the surface, it's a masterpiece of cosmic horror.

However, despite its themes inducing fear through impressively disturbing designs, it's a turn-based RPG where your decisions shape both the party and the story, which quickly spirals into madness.

Despite its modest origins in RPG Maker, the game compensates for its technical limitations with outstanding art and writing, aided by a functional gameplay component that ensures the campaign flows smoothly, so the protagonist—the atmosphere—never suffers in the slightest.

Look Outside is among the finest indie games of the last couple of years, although it seems the community hasn't quite grasped the greatness with which it represents the work of H.P. Lovecraft... Yet.

We all know that everything Obsidian touches turns to gold, though for reasons that are hard to understand, the gaming community seems to have overlooked this when it came to Alpha Protocol.

Yes, the action sequences are decent at best, and technically speaking, it's a subpar product, but the stealth, writing, and decision-making are so magnificent that I struggle to imagine a world where the negative outweighs the positive.

You can experience the story multiple times in diametrically opposed ways and have campaigns that feel unique, with memorable characters, plot points that truly make you think, and a worldbuilding that lures you to explore every last detail.

Since I know there are two types of RPG fans, one who prioritizes gameplay and another who prioritizes narrative, I must emphasize that only the latter will truly enjoy Alpha Protocol, though their lives will be completely changed once they play it.

From Mass Effect 2 to Elden Ring, these RPGs make putting off the main quest worthwhile—and sometimes even essential to the outcome.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance was a very pleasant surprise, but it appealed to a limited niche due to the specificity of its medieval setting. Therefore, I don't think any of us expected Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 to become the new gold standard for RPGs.

All future titles of this genre that prioritize immersion and the complexity of their systems will have to look to Warhorse Studios' masterpiece, which demands a titanic yet worthy effort to show why it's one of the finest works the genre has produced this decade.

By polishing absolutely everything from its predecessor and improving upon it as much as humanly possible, it's a perfect sequel that doesn't fall short in any area, being extraordinary in its narrative, gameplay, interactivity, audiovisuals, and even its overall atmosphere.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 is the blueprint that every first-person RPG should take into consideration for years to come, which is an astounding affirmation to say considering that the original was just very good.

Over the years, I've made it my mission to champion Dragon's Dogma as the most underrated video game of the century, and unfortunately, not even the sequel's success has allowed me to hang up my gloves in that endeavor.

Capcom has numerous masterpieces to its name, though this one in particular stands out for how far ahead of its contemporaries it was at its release, offering an epic fantasy scope barely explored by a couple of other titles within the genre in all its history.

The scale at which Gransys allows us to develop a heroic tale against colossal and captivating beasts is breathtaking, compelling you to lose yourself in a classic mythology that enchants you from its goblins to its dragons.

Thanks to the spectacular gameplay and customization options, where skirmishes are remarkably large and visually stunning regardless of the class you choose, it's a title that could hardly have been anticipated, especially considering what its competitors were doing at the time.

Years go by, and Dragon's Dogma keeps aging like the finest wine, waiting for the video game industry to finally recognize it as one of the past decade's generational titles.

#4360. Final Fantasy Resonance Review - On Its Own Wavelength

RPG publisher Square Enix has been doing the Lord's work lately by rescuing their discontinued mobile games and rehydrating them into full-fat RPG experiences. Last year's Octopath Traveler 0 is one such triumph, and it's safe to say Final Fantasy Resonance is another victory for reusing assets instead of throwing them in the garbage. More importantly, it's a great RPG experience with a fun cast and character customization options that will make fans of the Final Fantasy V job system rabid with delight.

Resonance is based on the first season of the now-defunct Final Fantasy Brave Exvius mobile game, which ran four chapters in total from 2016 to 2025, but Resonance is no mere port. For starters, it received an HD-2D injection that gussied up Exvius's already-impressive sprites. Resonance wears the HD-2D aesthetic confidently; Square Enix has obviously listened to past criticisms of its beloved graphical style, and it paid off. Resonance is an HD-2D game, but its highly detailed character sprites and occasional jaw-dropping pixel-based "cinema" scene differentiate it from the Octopath Traveler series and the Dragon Quest HD-2D remakes.

Resonance's distinctions are its greatest strength, in fact. It's easy to assume at first blush that its story about a boy and his best friend is nothing but a table to prop retro Final Fantasy references upon. It's true that a key part of Resonance's gameplay involves summoning "Visions" into battle, said visions being projections of characters from other Final Fantasy games. But that's all they are: Projections. They teach transferable skills, à la Final Fantasy V's job system. They can offer characters permanent stat boosts as they level up, like Final Fantasy VI's espers. And when conditions are met, they can be summoned to perform a super attack via a CGI spectacle that will remind you Square Enix have been masters of game cinema direction since day one.

Each Resonance character can equip a Vision that lends them their powers in a fight, and also grants passive upgrades and skills. Rain, for example, is a heavy hitter with innate fire attacks, but if he wears Cecil Harvey as a backpack, he also gets access to light and dark magic. Cecil gets stronger as they fight together, and bestows skills that can be equipped as wanted. If you're a Final Fantasy V job-head, you've come home.

But Final Fantasy Resonance is Rain's story despite its many callbacks to past games. Yes, Rain is an amalgamation of past Final Fantasy heroes, from Cloud's spiky yellow hair to Tidus's daddy issues, to Zidane's sunny attitude (with a hint of shadow), but that just makes him easier to root for. Rain's roommate, Lasswell, contains notes of my beloved Kain Highwind from Final Fantasy IV, but there's a troubled nobility to him that's purely his own. They're gradually joined by a cast of characters who click with each other (and thus, with me) thanks in part to comedic side-discussions delivered with quality voice acting. References to past Final Fantasy games are doled with clever subtlety. As a Final Fantasy XIV fan, I had to peel myself off the ceiling more than once when I encountered some choice shoutouts.

Resonance's battle system grants it another distinction. It's a classic turn-based system that shows off who's next in line to attack, like Final Fantasy X. Every character brings a fighting style and elemental flavor to the party. Lasswell is a samurai who favors ice, Jake is a gunner attuned to the wind, and Lid will rain the fattest of steel chocobos upon your head in an earth-based attack.

Resonance is a snappy game, which might be its most welcome trait. Fast travel is generous, and dungeons are conquered in just the right amount of time. You're looking at a 40-hour experience, give or take, which is downright digestible for an RPG in this day and age. On the flipside, Rain's world lacks depth. Its towns are beautiful, unique, and filled with characters and quest-givers who are worth talking to, but the overworld connective tissue is thin and its dungeons lack pizzazz. An auto-battle option would lessen the frustration of random encounters, but said encounters don't pop up nearly as often as they do in ancestral Final Fantasy games. Plus, the random battles are spaced in a way that makes grinding unnecessary unless you're maxing out a Vision, which I appreciate, but sometimes you're just trying to get to a place.

I went into Resonance expecting to like it for its salute to Final Fantasy characters across the decades, but I wound up loving the game for showing me a whole new canon. In a time when mainline Final Fantasy is still figuring itself out, Final Fantasy Resonance is easy to recommend. It has one foot planted on the solid foundation of Final Fantasy's history, but with its rich graphics and likeable cast of characters it builds up from that history instead of merely pillaging it.

#4359. Review: Wild Blue Skies (Switch) - An Unoriginal Alternative To Star Fox 64

Wild Blue Skies is Star Fox 64-lite. Gameplay, identity, story: everything is pretty much a license-free version of Star Fox 64. That isn’t necessarily a bad thing, but in a year with Star Fox (2026), a superb remake of the N64 classic, the question immediately becomes: Who is Wild Blue Skies for?

Stop me if this sounds familiar. Chuhai Labs' game — which, it should be said, was in development and announced long before the Switch 2 Star Fox remake was publicly known — stars a rag-tag gang of four pilots who, after being recruited by a general, need to travel across the skies to stop an evil exiled engineer from world domination.

This is unequivocally a carbon copy of Star Fox’s plot: Bowie, Chuck, Thorne, and Roe are your team Star Fox equivalent; The Prowlers are your Star Wolf stand-ins; and Grimclaw and Andross are practically the same one-note villain. Even dialogue and story beats are presented in the same iconic square-window boxes.

But where Star Fox shines in its character interactions and iconic lines, Wild Blue Skies falters. There is no personality, no charming moments, nothing to set the Blue Bombers apart from their Nintendo counterparts. They are all simply there because Star Fox 64 said so, leading to some of the most unmemorable interactions in recent memory.

Gameplay-wise, I could easily have copy-pasted the section from Jim's review of Star Fox (2026), and it would be equally applicable. The gameplay is virtually identical. You play as Bowie in his not-Arwing on a seven-stage adventure as you make your way to the evil Grimclaw’s base across the world map. Levels are predominantly on-rails as you and your teammates shoot down enemy after enemy until you reach the stage’s boss.

Along the way, some stages have secret objectives, leading to branching paths that change your path to the game’s final boss. And of course, a few stages shift the gameplay into all-range mode, giving you full 360-degree control in a dogfighting arena. Really, the only elements missing are the Landmaster and Blue Marine.

From controls, power-ups, level navigation, and even stage objectives, it really feels like the developers are one barrel-roll away from the Nintendo ninjas bursting in through their door. It also means that every complaint someone has with the original Star Fox 64 is likely present here, too.

The game is incredibly short, likely only taking you around two hours to beat. Your teammates sometimes can get in the way, just like Slippy famously does. And the difficulty can be incredibly punishing, as losing all your lives means starting over from scratch. Nothing here is inherently bad, but the lack of originality here is truly staggering.

Really, the only change to Star Fox worth mentioning (besides the absence of the other vehicles) comes in the level scoring system. Like the original, you gain points for every enemy you shoot down, but that won’t be enough to earn you the stage’s medal. Instead, you also have four “commendations” to complete as well: no damage taken, fast boss defeat, full squad survival, and collecting the four WILD letters hidden in the stage.

Achieving each commendation gives you an extra 50 points on top of your score, and completing at least a few of those in each stage is likely required to achieve the stage’s medal. In theory, this adds more replay value on such a short game, but in reality, it complicates Star Fox 64’s system that already worked well enough.

However, if there is one aspect of Wild Blue Skies that stands out, it’s in the production value. Visually, it uses a cell-shaded look that arguably looks better at times than Velan Studios' Switch 2 remake. The colours are incredibly vibrant and a treat to look at, as are some of the stage environments. While it would have been great to see some more environmental objects, like buildings or trees, what is there is sufficient.

The game runs incredibly well on Switch 2 hardware (although this is a Switch 1 release), and it’s also worth commending that all dialogue is completely voice-acted and features a fully animated intro cutscene.

Wild Blue Skies is what happens when a spiritual successor takes too much inspiration from its predecessor. There is nothing inherently wrong with the game, but if you have played Star Fox 64, or the remake, you have played Wild Blue Skies. As this is releasing on the original Switch, there is an argument to be made that it might tide over Star Fox fans who don’t have a Switch 2 yet. But with the original widely accessible on Nintendo Switch Online, it’s hard to see that argument holding much weight.

Wild Blue Skies is a perfectly average game, but with no originality, it makes for a hard recommendation, even to the most dedicated fans of Lylat's finest.

"The game is incredibly short, likely only taking you around two hours to beat."

Also, shmups and shooters sink or swim based on the quality of their level design, but I don't think that's even covered in this review? To be clear, I'm a big Star Fox fan, so if an imitation shows up with a bunch of well designed new levels to play, I'm in.

#4358. 6 JRPGs to Play If You Loved Final Fantasy Resonance

Murillo Zerbinatto is a JRPG enthusiast, writer, and editor. He has played over 300 RPGs during his gaming career, with 90% of them being JRPGs.

Final Fantasy Resonance is here, and it is already earning high praise from critics and players alike. Boasting an overwhelmingly positive score on Steam, the JRPG has been showered with acclaim for its combat systems, its compelling cast, and its triumphant return to Final Fantasy roots, serving as a love letter to fans of the franchise's 90s golden era.

If you cherished everything Rain and Lasswell's title brought to the table and want more, I have put together a list of other JRPGs to dive into if you enjoyed Final Fantasy Resonance. We have titles featuring modular Job systems, gorgeous pixel art, and secret-packed worlds that will extend your playtime far beyond the main story. It has never been a better time to be a JRPG fan.

Final Fantasy Resonance traces its lineage back to Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, and like many mobile gacha projects, it wears its mainline references and influences proudly. You know who else excels at wearing their JRPG influences on their sleeve? Indie developers. And speaking of phenomenal indie JRPGs, Chained Echoes is a masterclass. If you haven't played it yet, fix that immediately.

First off, Chained Echoes doesn't feature a traditional class system, so if that is your primary draw, the other entries on this list might suit you better. However, if you are looking for stunning pixel art, a gripping narrative, lovable characters, and a nostalgic trip down memory lane, whether through familiar tropes of yesteryear or simply the authentic feel of a 16-bit classic, you owe it to yourself to try Chained Echoes. Its turn-based combat loop is iconic, progression feels clean yet engaging, and its world exploration stands among the finest in the genre. It is thoroughly worth your time.

Plenty of hidden gems in the mobile world deserve a second chance.

Live A Live is delightfully unorthodox, and neither its combat layout nor its narrative structure shares much common ground with Final Fantasy Resonance. Their primary shared trait is the HD-2D visual engine. You might ask why I am recommending it here, and the answer comes down to character focus. Final Fantasy Resonance shines through its incredible cast, successfully translating gacha origins into a complete offline adventure by turning side characters into quest givers and granting them a well-deserved spotlight.

This often-overlooked SNES classic is entirely character-driven. At the start of the journey, you select from several distinct scenarios, each featuring its own protagonist, narrative arc, and setting. The structure feels episodic, but everything weaves together brilliantly by the end. Final Fantasy Resonance places that same heavy emphasis on its cast, so if character development was your favorite aspect, Live A Live will deliver in spades.

Fantasian might be one of the most underrated JRPGs on the market. Developed by Mistwalker under the direction of Hironobu Sakaguchi, the creator of Final Fantasy, Fantasian deserves far more mainstream recognition. Granted, the game originally debuted on a limited platform with Apple Arcade (where I first played it), but the release of Fantasian Neo Dimension brought it to consoles and PC, and you should definitely give it a shot.

Comparatively, the main parallel it shares with Final Fantasy Resonance is its turn-based foundation, though even the combat has its own distinct flavor. Fantasian introduces a unique trajectory targeting system where abilities feature varied area-of-effect paths. Each character follows their own skill tree, and while offering roughly three distinct build directions per party member, it lacks the deep modular customization of Resonance. Still, that comforting sense of playing a classic JRPG from a bygone era, bringing warmth to your heart as you revisit retro design sensibilities, is undisputed. If you want pure nostalgia, Fantasian is the way to go.

Our reviewer earned a platinum trophy and gave Final Fantasy Resonance a 10/10. Check out DualShockers' review of Final Fantasy Resonance.

One of my favorite parts of watching new players jump into Final Fantasy Resonance was seeing them unlock fresh Visions and map out synergy builds for their party. I could practically see the gears turning as they calculated which abilities would mesh best with each character. If that customization loop was your favorite part of the experience, I highly recommend picking up Bravely Default.

Any entry in the series will do, but both Bravely Default II and Bravely Default Flying Fairy HD Remaster will scratch that build-crafting itch (I personally find the second half of the original game a bit tedious, hence my primary recommendation for Bravely Default II). The Job system functions almost identically to Visions in Final Fantasy Resonance: the more you level up your Jobs, the wider your build options and combat potential become. Who knows, you might just discover your next favorite Bartz-style combo in Bravely Default.

If Final Fantasy Resonance left you feeling nostalgic, it is only fitting to revisit the pinnacle of pixel remaster releases. This is doubly true if you have yet to play Final Fantasy VI, as you will recognize countless references while discovering why so many fans rank the sixth entry as the franchise's absolute peak. Final Fantasy VI is simultaneously accessible and deeply complex across all of its design layers.

The combat uses the classic Active Time Battle system, but each party member has unique innate strengths that can be further customized through Espers. The story avoids focusing on a single protagonist, instead distributing screen time across an ensemble cast to build a living, captivating world. During the game's second half, the path forward is left entirely in your hands. Ultimately, you will get to experience one of the true masterpieces of the JRPG genre, or reconnect with it if you have not checked out the Pixel Remaster edition yet.

Final Fantasy Resonance proves that classic Final Fantasy ideas still work, from turn-based combat and jobs to overworld exploration and dungeons.

The most obvious choice on this list is Octopath Traveler II. While I still suggest playing the original first to avoid getting too comfortable with the sequel's refinements, nothing stops you from diving straight into the second title. Octopath Traveler II takes the foundation established by Square Enix's inaugural HD-2D release and elevates every aspect, from storytelling and combat mechanics to visual polish.

Octopath Traveler II previously held the highest review score for an HD-2D title before Final Fantasy Resonance arrived, which speaks volumes about both games' quality. Both titles offer unmatched character customization, with the Visions in Final Fantasy Resonance mirroring the flexibility, dynamism, and build variety found in Octopath Traveler II's Job system. It offers more HD-2D charm, more heart, and endless fun

Craving more turn-based JRPGs after Final Fantasy Resonance? These 10 games offer everything from classic systems to modern twists.

#4357. Here's A Recap Of The October 2026 ID@Xbox Showcase

If you're an Xbox owner looking for new indie games to play, today's ID@Xbox showcase provided 30 minutes of new, upcoming, and existing indie games coming to Microsoft's platforms. We've rounded up every announcement here for a quick recap of the event.

2 Ton Studios, creators of 2020's Unto the End, announced this atmospheric sci-fi title about surviving a harsh exoplanet. For you and your crew to survive, you must scavenge resources while enduring injury and radiation. You'll also have to battle what appear to be giant alien sea urchins.

Frogs are the de facto mascot of the indie scene, and Croak, a hand-drawn 2D platformer, keeps this unofficial tradition alive. As the Frog Prince, you'll use your lengthy and sticky tongue to grapple up platforms and propel yourself forward, then roll into a ball to bounce onto and between objects like an amphibian Sonic the Hedgehog.

Developer Glee-Cheese Studio treated viewers to a full look at one of the game's many music-based platforming levels.

This hand-drawn search action game about an editor trapped inside an unfinished manuscript is coming to Xbox after previously being announced for PS5 and PC.

Developer Titan1Studios describes Love is a Roguelike as "50 First Dates meets Edge of Tomorrow", which is quite an intriguing combination of story premises. This deck-building strategy sci-fi western stars a Rex, a rogue space marshal, and his partner, Lakshmi, who must recover the shattered memories of the latter while trapped in a time loop on an asteroid.

This blend of roguelike deckbuilding and tower defense tasks players with stripping fully destructible worlds of their riches while protecting your Planetary Drill by erecting fortresses and other defenses.

This sinister deckbuilder sees you gamble your life for cash in the deadly corporate office of Mr. Magpie, a deranged puppet voiced by Matt Mercer. You're trapped, so to climb the corporate ladder, you must strategically flip cards, stack your deck, take advantage of synergies, and, whatever you do, avoid Jerry cards.

There's no shortage of indie creature collecting games, but Waveling Island aims to win fans over with its hand-drawn pixel art, cozy vibes, and tropical island backdrop. After washing ashore, you'll capture, train, and battle various strange creatures (e.g., a sentient pencil) while befriending the island's residents and unraveling a big mystery. You can also rebuild the island by gathering resources to construct and decorate buildings.

The multiplayer sequel to the minimalist viral hit A Game About Digging a Hole is, like its 2025 predecessor, exactly what it sounds like. Up to four friends can now work together to dig a big hole, only this time it's on a beach. You can unlock new digging equipment, find treasure, and collect and sell resources to keep your dig going as deep as possible.

Formerly known as Scramble Knights Royale, the game’s focus has shifted to focus on co-op exploration in a shared world with other players. This MMO-lite features dungeons to crawl, monsters to slay, and loot to find for those looking for a multiplayer take on classic Zelda.

Another game that's exactly what it sounds like: you must shred confidential company documents to earn a $1 million payout. Destroying towering paper stacks becomes an easier task thanks to the moral support of the constantly-watching, toxically positive "Happiness Manager".

This dark fantasy RPG centers on a human slaving away in the Demon Realm who rebels against his captors. The third-person Souls-like action looks bloody and brutal, though genre fans probably wouldn't want it any other way.

Set in a post-apocalyptic world wiped out by the "idiot virus", the protagonist receives a letter from their long-missing father to kick off a search for answers. The story-driven action games challenge players to survive slums filled with infected citizens in a narrative centered on finding life and kindness in a broken world.

The team behind Herald: The Interactive Period Drama tells a decidedly more fantastical tale about dispatching a team of vampires in Cold War-era Berlin. To succeed in this tactical narrative RPG, you must navigate choice-driven scenarios to earn the trust of your undead teammates and use their powers to determine the destiny of your house.

After the greatest female pilot goes missing, players control a headache-suffering detective searching for her whereabouts. The top-down adventure sees players gather clues, solve puzzles, and regularly take medication to remedy their persistent headache. You'll also battle enemies with over eight weapons, including a cane, umbrella, and crossbow.

Zero Parades: For Dead Spies, the spiritual follow-up to Disco Elysium, only launched in May, but it already has a much-improved Director's Cut coming next month. This version features new scenes adding over 40,000 words), a backstage mode, a new dramatic encounter, voice-over improvements, new clothing items, a new death screen, inventory filtering, and more. While the update has been available for the existing versions of the game on PS5 and PC, it will be the default version when it comes to Xbox.

PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2, Switch, PC

Check out a new story trailer for the upcoming remaster of one of Telltale Games' most celebrated adventures ahead of its launch in a couple of weeks.

PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2, Switch, PC

The cult-favorite movie tie-in to Shrek 2 is being remastered courtesy of Aspyr. If you missed the 2004 game, it features Shrek, Donkey, Fiona, and other familiar faces battling evil in solo or co-op play for up to four players (local and online). The remaster boasts improved visuals, new features such as a photo mode, and the ability to swap characters instantly.

#4356. Vampirio is a rogue-like action RPG that lets you build by day and slay monsters at night — here are 5 reasons to sink your teeth into it

Outfit7, the publisher behind Talking Tom & Friends, has just launched Vampirio, a rogue-like action RPG that combines monster-slaying combat with fortress-building and nightly survival battles. Here are five reasons to take a closer look. A familiar character…with a twist Before there was Dracula, there was Vlad Dracul, a young monster hunter whose life is torn apart by loss. Vampirio explores the events that set him on a path of vengeance toward becoming the legendary vampire.

You’ll discover his story while battling waves of monsters in a vibrant, top-down world. With different playable heroes and rogue-like progression adding variety to each run, there’s more to surviving the night than simply slaying everything in sight.

Nine heroes, different ways to fight Vampirio features nine playable heroes, each bringing different abilities and a distinct combat style.

The first hero you’ll play is Alba, who introduces you to the fundamentals before more heroes become available. As you unlock characters including Vlad, Lucian, and Morana, experiment to find the playstyles that suit you.

Whether you prefer ranged attacks, close-range combat, or powerful magic, switching heroes can change how you approach a fight and which upgrades you choose.

Brains over brawn Surviving monster-filled nights requires more than a strong roster of heroes, and this is where Vampirio’s base-building elements come into play.

During the day, gather resources, expand your fortress, and build or upgrade walls and defensive towers. When night falls, those preparations are put to the test as your hero fights alongside your defences.

From skeletons to dragons and powerful bosses, each night brings fresh threats to overcome. Careful preparation can make the difference between holding the line and watching your defences crumble.

Rogue-like progression Every run offers opportunities to experiment with different skills and upgrades, encouraging you to adapt your strategy as the challenge unfolds. Randomised upgrades keep encounters fresh, meaning you can't rely on the same approach every time.

That doesn't mean you're starting from scratch after every defeat, though. Permanent progression gives you ways to grow stronger between runs, while developing your heroes adds another layer of long-term strategy,

You’ll also collect enemy stickers by defeating monsters and bosses. Completing sticker collections unlocks lasting progression bonuses, giving you another way to strengthen future runs.

Raid rival fortresses — and risk revenge Not all your resource-gathering has to happen at home. Vampirio also lets you raid other players' fortresses, offering another way to gather supplies.

Destroying buildings and looting resources can help you climb the lifetime rankings, but there's a catch: your targets can retaliate with revenge attacks. Raiding therefore comes with a risk, especially when you already have your hands full defending against the creatures of the night.

You'll need to weigh the rewards against the potential consequences as you decide how aggressively to expand your resources and strengthen your fortress.

Vampirio is available to download now on iOS, Android and Steam. As an extra bit of fun, you can also find out which hero matches you best by taking the Vampirio personality quiz: https://vampirio.app/quiz

#4355. Arc Raiders just keeps breaking its own Steam player records

Word of mouth has done wonders for the popularity of Arc Raiders, clearly more than all the pre-launch marketing and hype.

Arc Raiders just cannot be stopped. The extraction shooter from Embark Studios has once again attracted more players over the weekend than it has in its launch week, and over its first weekend on the market.

The positive reception the PvPvE game has garnered from players has clearly caused many of them to convince their friends to jump into this unique gem of a game.

The day Arc Raiders launched, it peaked at 264,673 concurrent players on Steam. Although not massive, it was quite a bit more than the game’s most popular - free - beta test managed to attract.

That figure was broken yet again over the game’s first weekend, with Arc Raiders having reached 354,836 concurrent players on Steam. This is where many thought it would settle, as we start to see the gradual - and expected - decline of player numbers.

To everyone’s surprise, however, Arc Raiders shattered even that record yet again on Sunday, November 9. According to SteamDB, the game peaked at 462,488 concurrent players on Steam, which is a sizeable increase on its launch day numbers. Indeed, should this trend continue, Arc Raiders is going to be well on its way to doubling its initial launch record.

While a few games have broken their launch Steam player records in the past, it’s incredibly rare to see it happen - especially twice in such a short period after launch. Embark clearly has a winner on its hands here.

Arc Raiders’ next big moment is the game’s first post-launch map, which is set to arrive at some point this month, alongside new Quests and other gameplay items. Seeing as how the Steam concurrent record has been broken twice, there’s every chance the arrival of the new map will bring another boost to player numbers.

If you’re among the millions of players who have been exploring the Rust Belt, you’re probably wondering where to find prickly pears, where to find lemons and apricots, and where to find olives - and those links will answer all of those questions. And, if you just jumped in over the weekend, you’re definitely going to find these Arc Raiders tips very helpful.

#4354. 10 Legendary Weapons You Should Have in Borderlands 4

Aden Carter is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2020. He specializes in lists and guides, with a focus on RPGs, horror games, survival horror, Soulslikes, cozy/sim games, and action-adventure titles. Before joining DualShockers, Aden contributed to GameRant, XDA, Gamepur, I

Borderlands 4 has a lot of legendary weapons. With the first entire year of content for the game being done, there are now over 160 different legendary weapons that you can choose from.

This only covers the actual weapons, like legendary assault rifles and shotguns, and not the grenades, shields, and class mods you can get. When choosing a weapon, there is a lot to consider.

At this point, there are several weapons that you should have in your bank or on your character that have stayed consistently strong. If you don’t have these weapons, you should probably start farming for them in case there are future DLC plans.

Crow-Sourced is not a legendary weapon, but I am counting it anyone because it is a Pearlescent and they are more rare than legendary items in Borderlands 4. This weapon is one of the Pearlescent weapons added with the first DLC titled Mad Ellie and the Vault of the Damned.

To obtain this assault rifle, you need to make your way over to the Captain Willis boss fight in The Maelstrom. In other words, you won’t get it until the end of the DLC, but it is well worth the wait.

This weapon has the Left of the Murder ability, which makes it fire out random projectiles as you shoot it. Charging the weapon increases the number of projectiles, making it more lethal the more it is charged.

Captain Willis will give you a run for your money in the Mad Ellie and the Vault of the Damned DLC for Borderlands 4.

The Swan Song is one of those weapons that you can use to clear a room very quickly, which means it is a guarantee that you should have it on your characters. This weapon fires fast, hits hard, and even shoots cannonballs.

That’s right, you read that correctly, it first cannonballs. Thanks to its Cannonball ability, you can shoot out cannonballs from the underbarrel of this weapon. Each kill with this weapon grants additional cannonballs, with four being the maximum.

As a weapon, the Swan Song is very powerful, but the underbarrel packs a massive punch, so it is important to continuously use it as you take down enemies. Speaking of takedowns, you get this weapon from the Takedown at Hadron Abyss.

The Darkbeast is one of my go-to weapons when I create a new character. I have a level 30 version of this weapon for new characters, and I always make sure to get one at max level as well for each character.

This SMG packs a serious punch, with it often outperforming other weapons that I use on my characters. Its Parley ability makes it so bullets pierce enemies, and have a 5% chance to cause an explosion when they hit an enemy.

Thanks to this weapon's amazing fire rate, that 5% seems to proc very often, causing major damage. You will never be let down by the Darkbeast, and you can get it from Voraxis in the Coastal Bonescape.

With how I mentioned that the Darkbeast tends to outperform other weapons, there are some that still outperform it, and the Ohm I got is one of them. This is an electric legendary SMG that fires a laser at opponents, and it will absolutely destroy shields.

It has the ability Energy Transfer, which boosts its damage by 50% whenever your shield is active. However, it consumes your shield in the process. This can be prevented if you have an overshield, so any character can get massive damage with this weapon if they just have an overshield.

The best part about this ability, besides the damage, is that it doesn’t consume ammo when you have a shield either, allowing it to fire infinitely until your shield is gone. You can get this weapon from the second Ripper Queen fight.

If you want a weapon that can delete a boss’s health bar, look no further than the Hot Slugger. A few shots from this can annihilate a health bar if you have the right build.

This legendary shotgun has the Blazing Barrel ability, which gives it a 30% damage boost for 10 seconds after you get a kill. This can stack up to three times for a massive 90% damage boost if you keep getting kills.

You can stack this damage during a boss fight by killing minions and then destroy the boss’s health bar. There are multiple builds that can take advantage of this weapon, and it is amazing.

The Convergence has been around since the start of Borderlands 4 and it still stands as one of the best legendary shotguns in the game, and it is one that you can get relatively easily. It is also a gun that can carry you through many hardships.

This weapon has the Asymptotic ability, which it doesn’t give an explanation for, but you can easily tell what it does as soon as you fire the weapon. Every time you hit an enemy, additional shots converge onto that enemy dealing additional damage.

This causes the weapon to deal some massive damage to enemies. Combined with its fast fire rate, you can easily wipe out health bars in no time. This weapon is dropped from Bramblesong in the Bittervein Augur Mine.

There are many bosses in Borderlands 4, but only Bramblesong has the Convergence as a dedicated drop.

Don’t you just wish that your guns had triple the bullets that you could embed into the bodies of your enemies? Well, the Triplicate, one of the best DLC weapons, aims to deliver, as it will indeed fill your enemies full of lead.

This weapon has the Tripled ability, which makes it so additional explosive projectiles get lobbed whenever you hit an enemy. This makes the weapon overpowered, and capable of taking down groups of enemies in record time.

If you manage to get a shotgun alternate fire mode on this weapon, it will score multiple hits, allowing multiple projectiles to spawn out of the enemy, and when used against larger enemies, it is a death sentence. You can get this weapon from The Reject Prototype in the Amara and the Vile Shadow DLC.

The Golden God is amazing as long as you don’t mind continuously buying ammo for it, as it will use a ton of ammo. However, that ammo loss is okay since you will annihilate every enemy you look at.

The ability Rage make it so that the Golden Gun does not break when you hit the heat threshold. Instead, it continuously consumes greater and greater amounts of ammo until you eventually run out.

This allows you to continuously output damage at an impressive rate, but you will just use a ton of ammo in the process. This weapon can be obtained by farming Idolator Sol, which is one of the earlier bosses in the game.

Stray is a legendary sniper rifle that was available from the get-go when Borderlands 4 launched. All you needed to do was make your way over to the Tendercage Ripper Drill Site and kill the boss called Pango Bango.

Pango Bango drops three weapons, but Stray is by far the best of them. This legendary sniper rifle has the ability stray, which makes it fire two secondary bullets that home in on nearby targets.

This makes it great for clearing out crowds, and one of the best sniper rifles in the game. It is a weapon, like the others on this list, that works very well with most builds, and can be utilized by any of the characters effortlessly.

At this point, everyone should have the Bod in either their bank or on their character, as this weapon is fantastic, and is amazing for testing out builds. The reason is that is counts as every type of weapon.

The All-Arounder ability on it makes it so that it counts as a shotgun, assault rifle, sniper rifle, pistol, and SMG. This also means that it is affected by every type of damage increase, even for specific weapon types.

Even more, the damage bonuses can stack, meaning you can get the benefit of skills that increase damage for SMGs and shotguns on this weapon. To obtain the Bod, you will want to farm Axemaul in Carcadia Burn district of Dominion.

#4353. Battlefield 6 patch finally ends the menace of the Lock-Guided Missile, shuts down the Recon Drone Sledgehammer exploit and more

Today's Battlefield 6 patch is laser-focused on taking care of some of the more infuriating bugs while also taking out a couple of exploits.

The next Battlefield 6 update is here. Having gone live just moments ago, update 1.1.1.5 is something of a midseason update, bringing a few quality of life tweaks to the game alongside some key fixes for a few of the issues that cropped up since the launch of Season 1 in late October.

This latest release is also the first to tackle some of the problems players have been running into playing Redsec battle royale, the free-to-play component that also came out recently.

Patch 1.1.1.5 is fairly limited in scope. The biggest fix in this one comes to the Lock-Guided Missiles going through flares, and generally being annoying enough to stop players from using air vehicles altogether.

The Lock-Guided Missiles were mainly used by AA vehicles, but they could also be equipped by IFVs, which made it even more of a nightmare to pilots. It got so bad that Battlefield Studios disabled it entirely while the team worked on a proper fix.

Another exploit the patch fixes is the one that allowed players to stand on the Recon Drone and reach areas they’re not supposed to. This was done by… repeatedly hitting it with a Sledgehammer. The long-running issue of vehicles not spawning for certain teams in Conquest and Breakthrough appears to have finally been fixed, too.

In terms of battle royale, the patch has a few fixes that should help make the experience more consistent, as well as improve the flow of matches. One of the more interesting addresses an issue that could eliminate the entire squad instead of reviving dead teammates when using a Mobile Spawn.

Patch 1.1.1.5 also has yet more adjustments to weapon dispersion (bloom). Some of the casses it addresses include transitioning from sprint to firing in ADS, and others where it apparently scaled with player movement speed.
