#4339. Battlefield 6 is getting a free trial next week with... a questionable selection of maps, but at least the modes are good

If Redsec got you hooked on Battlefield gameplay but you never experienced traditional multiplayer in Battlefield 6, there's an upcoming moment you might want to pay attention to.

Presumably as a way of marching ever forward towards its (alleged) 100 million player goal for Battlefield 6, EA has announced that the multiplayer shooter will be getting its first free trial later this month.

This is, of course, specifically for players to sample the core, paid component of the game, as the recently launched Redsec remains free-to-play. Redsec, however, offers modes like battle royale and Gauntlet, which aren’t quite the traditional Battlefield experience.

The Battlefield 6 trial arrives next Tuesday, November 25. It will run for one week, ending the following Tuesday, December 2. The trial will be available on all platforms, but won’t include all content from the full game.

Instead, players will have access to three of the game’s maps and five of its modes. Siege of Cairo will be there alongside Season 1’s two new maps: Eastwood, and Blackwell Fields. It’s not the strongest line-up of maps, considering Eastwood is already cut from the larger Fort Lyndon battle royale map that Redsec players should be quite familiar with, but it’s something.

As for modes, you can pick from Conquest, Breakthrough, Sabotage, and Team Deathmatch. Battlefield Studios didn’t say what the fifth mode is going to be, but a dedicated blog post with more information is set to arrive next week.

Beyond the trial's content itself, the timing is certainly great. Battlefield 6 just received one of its biggest patches, kicking off the second phase of its first season. So far this season, we’ve seen two new maps, several new weapons - but more importantly, solutions to problems the game’s had since launch, as well as fixes to longstanding bugs.

The miserable XP progression Battlefield 6 launched with is far more tolerable. Challenges and Assignments are much easier to understand and actually finish. The often maligned weapon dispersion has been toned down. Some of the wildest vehicle bugs have been fixed. And Portal has a host of experiences that go beyond just bot farms.

In essence, Battlefield 6 feels like its reached its 1.0 status, which makes this a great entry point for new players, even if the trial could've used more of the game's better maps.

#4337. The Blood Of Dawnwalker Update 1.1 Adds Quality Of Life Improvements, Boosts Performance, and Adds Pettable Animals

We've been enjoying The Blood of Dawnwalker, one of the year's biggest games, but its release was a little rough around the edges. It took a lot of feedback from fans for developer Rebel Wolves to prioritize higher framerates at launch for consoles, but even then, the game certainly struggled at times on my PlayStation 5. Today, the game's first major update drops, and it aims to smooth some of those performance issues and introduce a few quality-of-life features.

The trailer above highlights combat-specific improvements, like improved targeting and animations, and a less restrictive camera. Rebel Wolves is also lowering the health of wolves and boars, who previously remained tanky even into the later hours of the game, and it should be easier to disengage from combat, should you choose to do so. For casual players, there's a new difficulty mode; what was previously "Story" mode has been renamed "Forgiving," while the new version of "Story" mode adds additional combat assists.

Rebel Wolves has also added some new features outside of combat. A new Daught of Mind Rebirth potion allows you to respec your skill tree, re-allocating time and skill points spent to switch up your build. You can also increase the size of subtitles (an option I'm always grateful for) and pet dogs and cats. Finally, the Shadowstep and Planeshift systems should be more responsive now – here's hoping I have an easier time teleporting onto rooftops instead of the wall right below them.

Those are the major, most visible highlights, but players can view the full patch notes here to see the hundreds of other minor improvements that aim to squash bugs, reduce crashes, and improve stability.

For more on The Blood of Dawnwalker, you can check out our review, in which our reviewer admires the swings the developers took, even though they don't always pay off. You can also check out our coverage hub for our issue devoted to The Blood of Dawnwalker, including interviews with its ex-Witcher development team.

#4336. Battlefield 6 streamlines some of the most annoying Challenges yet again, takes out a few of them entirely

The easier and more accessible Battlefield Studios makes those Battlefield 6 Challenges, the better.

The work to continue streamlining Challenges in Battlefield 6 is clearly not done. Having just released a new patch - which already included several updates to Challenges and Assignments - Battlefield Studios has gone in and made even more changes.

This latest round includes far fewer tweaks, but quite surprisingly, it also removes a few of the more annoying ones from the game.

The updated list, which Battlefield shared on Twitter, includes changes to the dreaded Recon 2 headshots beyond 150m Challenge. Now, any headshot beyond 75m will count. Recon Expert 3 is another headshot-themed one that’s been updated, and now requires getting headshot kills beyond 125m, rather than the practically impossible beyond 200m that it required previously.

The Rapid Fire 2 Challenge, which required getting kills beyond 50m with Assault Rifles, has been changed so it now tracks anything beyond 40m. The painful ‘Inflict damage under 15m while hip-firing with Assault Rifles’ has been entirely replaced with one that requires - the far more sensible - inflicting damage while in ADS with Assault Rifles.

A couple of Challenges, such as the one that required suppressing enemies with LMGs, and another that wanted you to deal damage to laser-designated vehicles using lock-on weapons, have both been removed.

The journey to make Challenges and Assignments easier to complete has been a long one. Progression has been one of the key areas of criticism Battlefield 6 received at launch. The issue encompassed more than just slow player and weapon XP earn rates, it also prevented players from accessing new Training Paths for the various classes, and several of the game's weapons.

Battlefield Studios attacked the problem from multiple angles, initially boosting the XP players and their weapons would earn, before later reducing the requirements of the Challenges themselves. The developer continued to streamline those requirements over multiple patches, including majorly overhauling the system earlier this month.

It seems the studio is more confident than ever in the game, as it recently announced that Battlefield 6 will be getting its first free trial next week, offering players who do not own the full game access to iconic modes like Conquest, and Breakthrough - though on an unusual selection of maps.

#4335. Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered Review: Absolute Kaiju Chaos

Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered delivers chaotic kaiju battles and couch co-op fun, even if its story and side features are thin.

72 years ago, the world was first introduced to the King of the Monsters, Godzilla, in the revolutionary 1954 kaiju film simply titled Godzilla, and since then the reptilian monster has gone on to appear in dozens of movies, shows, comics, and even video games.

While most of Godzilla’s video game appearances debuted in the 1980s and 1990s, the radioactive monster has made a few notable gaming manifestations in the early 2000s and 2010s, with a fan-favorite being 2002’s Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee.

Godzilla: DAMM turned out to be such a popular sixth generation console title that it not only spawned two sequels but a complete Unreal Engine 5 remaster for modern platforms called Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered.

Looking for new fighting games in 2026? Here are 10 upcoming fighters to watch, including indie gems, arena brawlers, and Godzilla.

To give a little bit of a background on myself with this title, I have never actually played the original Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee before nor any Godzilla game for that matter. I didn’t become a fan of or really understand Godzilla’s cultural importance until high school, around the time when Legendary Pictures’ Godzilla film was coming out coinciding with the franchise’s 60th anniversary.

The success of that film and its later Monsterverse sequels opened the door for me and a whole new generation of fans to become invested in Godzilla and his related kaiju, and seemingly to help capitalize on this new fan base, Atari and Pipeworks have decided to remaster DAMM for modern platforms.

Unlike other remasters, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered isn’t a simple HD port of the original 2002 game but is rather a sort of remake of the original, with Pipeworks having rebuilt the game in Unreal Engine 5 complete with enhanced visuals and modern quality of life improvements.

Pipeworks strived to keep Remastered’s core premise and gameplay as close to the original 2002 game as possible, with the remaster still featuring up to four-player local co-op, Adventure Mode, Destruction Mode, Survival Mode, and Practice Mode.

Pipeworks strived to keep Remastered’s core premise and gameplay as close to the original 2002 game as possible

For the first time ever, Remastered allows DAMM players to fight and play together across great distances thanks to the introduction of online multiplayer.

The game even features updated cutscenes primarily seen in Adventure Mode, with the cutscenes featuring the alien Vortaak being fairly reminiscent of the updated cutscenes in the 2020 Destroy All Humans! remake, especially with how both utilized 1950s-inspired sci-fi movie music.

The premise of Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is the alien Vortaak have come to Earth and mind-controlled most of the planet’s kaiju to wreck the planet and prepare it for a complete Vortaak invasion. One monster is somehow able to break free of the Vortaak’s control and sets out to defeat all of the other monsters and ultimately the Vortaak themselves.

This storyline is primarily depicted in the remaster’s Adventure Mode, with players being able to select from 12 monsters to play as including:

All of these monsters previously appeared in the original Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee save for the first version of Mechagodzilla who replaced Mechagodzilla 2 in the remaster.

1990s Godzilla, Anguirus, Megalon, and Gigan are all available to play as from the get-go while every other monster has to be unlocked by progressing through G-Force Research Rumors and Projects (not to be confused with the 2009 guinea pig spy movie G-Force).

At the game’s core, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is primarily centered around sandbox fights between two, three, or four monsters, with each monster featuring their own unique moveset that they can use to fight other monsters, destroy cities, and wipe out military units.

These fighting games' story modes allow people to play as villains instead of traditional heroes, often with destructive results.

For example, Megalon can use his drill-like front appendages to not only strike at enemies and buildings but also to burrow underground to pop back up at enemies and unleash a devastating blow sending monsters hurling through the air.

In this regard, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is a ton of fun to play and unlock each monster, with learning each monster’s moveset to use in local or online multiplayer being particularly fun.

1990s Godzilla, Anguirus, Megalon, and Gigan are all available to play as from the get-go

However, aside from unlocking every monster and playing through Adventure Mode with each monster, there’s not much incentive to keep on playing the game for long. Sure, players can unlock G-Force sighting video clips, monster photos but there’s no system to customize the monsters and most maps play far too similar to each other.

I can barely tell the difference between most cities aside from a few notable landmarks like Seattle’s space needle. That's okay though as the remaster is clearly not trying to reinvent the wheel or even include features from DAMM’s sequels since this is a remaster first and foremost, not a proper reimagining or a true sequel.

While I didn’t play Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee growing up, I can immediately feel the sixth console generation charm of the game from its remasters right from the start. It’s a fighting game that people can instantly have a ton of fun playing through as they wreak havoc throughout some of the planet's most famous cities and fight against some of cinema’s most famous monsters in single-player or comedic local or online matches.

With how uncommon it is to find brand-new local co-op games these days, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered feels like a breath of fresh air and it’s a game that young Godzilla fans will certainly want to pick up before the year’s end. Plus, with how affordable the remaster is both in terms of its price and its remarkably small file size, DAMMR is a game that any fan of Godzilla or fun couch co-op games in general should pick up soon as it will likely make for fantastic holiday gift. DAMMR might not have all that of an engaging story or even a ton of side features but it more than makes up for those flaws by being a simple fun game to create kaiju chaos solo or with friends.

#4333. Arc Raiders patch nerfs the Deadline mine, ends the menace of the Venator

The first post-Stella Montis patch for Arc Raiders has arrived, and it predictably touches much of what people brought to the latest map.

Arc Raiders has received a new update today that’s almost entirely dedicated to balance and economy tweaks. Patch 1.3.0 arrived earlier across all platforms, coming in at just under 1GB. This is an especially interesting patch because many of the changes it makes can be seen as a response to player behaviour on Stella Montis, the game’s latest map, which just joined the roster last week.

Stella Montis is available for players who’ve put in a decent number of rounds, and its close-quarters, enclosed environments have essentially turned it into the new “PvP map”, where constant action can be found.

That, of course, also means that the map has exposed a few balance issues with some of the game’s weapons and tools. Case in point: the Venator, a pistol that saw a lot of use recently. The weapon is especially powerful when fully-upgraded, something Arc Raiders developer Embark said pushed it beyond what had been originally intended.

In today’s update, the Venator's fire rate is the thing getting hit the hardest, with each upgrade now offering slower gains to the weapon's rate-of-fire compared to the way things were. The weapon’s weight is also being increased to five from two.

Another powerful item players have been getting a lot of mileage out of recently has been the Deadline mine. Unlike the Venator, the Deadline is mainly a threat to Arc enemies, and it’s proven incredibly powerful against the largest and most fearsome, such as the Bastion, and Leaper. In fact, the mine was considered essential when taking down a Queen.

The patch vastly increases its purchase price, and makes it more difficult to craft by upping the amount each of its components requires. Perhaps the most effective nerf, however, is the reduction to the Deadline’s stock at traders from three to just one, which means you’re going to be seeing a lot less of it topside.

Beyond those specific changes, Embark has also tweaked explosive damage across the board. According to the developer, explosive damage was being applied to multiple parts at once, which trivialised some encounters.

This change mainly affects larger Arc units, such as the Bastion, allowing them to withstand more explosive damage before bits start coming off of them. The Hullcracker, one of the best explosive damage weapons, has also caught a nerf as part of that.

Check the official blog for the full change log for patch 1.3.0. If you’re just getting started with the hottest extraction shooter ever, our Arc Raiders tips offer plenty of help. You should also learn what all the different Map Conditions do in Arc Raiders, and how to best make use of each of them.

#4332. Dispatch's Anniversary Update Brings Commentary Track, Storyboard Mode, And Mobile Port

Dispatch, a superhero-themed workplace comedy from last year, celebrates its one-year anniversary today. While it was released episodically, the first batch dropped on October 22. It was received well, with strong performances from a star-studded cast (including Breaking Bad star Aaron Paul) and filled a niche left vacant by Telltale Games' absence from the gaming world in recent years. Today, developer AdHoc announced a batch of anniversary content, and some of it drops today.

First, there's a new way to play Dispatch: storyboard mode. This option lets you play through the whole experience using the original animatics – rough placeholder sketches that the artists used to sync images up to the voice-over. It's a fun behind-the-scenes look at the game's development that we don't get very often. In that same vein, the cast and crew recorded DVD-style commentary tracks to play over the game, making jokes and sharing insight into the development process. A press release says there are over 16 hours of commentary from the game's development team (like art director Derek Stratton and creative directors Dennis Lenart and Nick Herman) as well as some of the cast, including Aaron Paul, Laura Bailey, and Erin Yvette.

Storyboard and Commentary modes are included in the game's deluxe edition, which you can upgrade to for $10.99. Both modes are available today.

If you haven't played the game yet, AdHoc has announced a new way to do so; Dispatch is coming to mobile platforms on December 9. It's been rebuilt to support touch controls and vertical play, and it will be available on iOS and Android. You can even play the first half of the game for free – the first four episodes are included, but you'll need to pay $19.99 to play the rest.

Finally, AdHoc announced new merch, including a book created alongside publisher Lost in Cult called Dispatch: Design Works, which is both an art book and a "making-of" book. There's also a live game soundtrack concert in Los Angeles featuring Thot Squad, Bershy, Primer, Caroline Kingsbury, Fartbarf, and Dispatch composer Andrew Arcadi with the SDN Company Band. It will be held at Avalon Hollywood on December 3, but it won't be livestreamed, so you'll need to grab a ticket to see the event. The press release states that people who signed up for updates from adhocstudio.com will be the first in line to purchase tickets.

#4331. Battlefield 6 may have actually done it: beaten Call of Duty

Battlefield 6 sales are setting all kinds of records, but one in particular has long eluded the Battlefield series.

If you’ve been paying any attention to the shooter market these past few months, you won’t be surprised to learn that Battlefield 6 has been an unprecedented success for EA, and the Battlefield series as a whole.

The game managed to sell over 7 million units at launch, climbing to the top of the charts anywhere you look, including setting new series concurrent player records on Steam. Thanks to new data, we now better understand the true scale of this launch.

The latest Circana report, which looks at game and hardware sales in the United States, has arrived. This iteration covers the month of October, which is when Battlefield 6 was released.

Battlefield 6 was the top-selling game across all platforms during October - which isn’t surprising. It has overtaken NBA 2K26 to become 2025’s best-selling game year-to-date, making it the best-selling Battlefield game ever.

In October alone, the game sold more than the lifetime sales of Battlefield 1, previously the best-selling entry in the franchise.

Battlefield 6 even set records beyond just its own series, having now produced the highest single-month dollar sales (physical and digital) total for any full game released in the last three years. The previous record holder was 2022’s Modern Warfare 2.

November’s report, which is set to arrive midway through December, will show, once and for all, whether Battlefield 6 has been able to overtake Black Ops 7. With one exception, Call of Duty games have, for more than a decade, topped the best-selling year-to-date chart. Regardless of the quality of the individual titles, or the competition in any given year, nothing has been able to shake that dominance.

Given all this momentum, Battlefield 6 has a shot at dethroning Call of Duty this year, beating Black Ops 7 to become the year’s best-seller. You never want to count out the sheer popularity of Call of Duty among casual players, however, which is what’s going to make December’s report all the more interesting.

#4330. Off the AppStore: Bless the fans, bless Undertale Vs Gojo

Welcome to Off The AppStore, a weekly feature with a twist. Namely, while these - as with all the games we cover here - are games that you can play on your phone, they're ones that operate outside of the realms of the big two ways to play: The Google Play Store and the Apple AppStore.

That means that there might be a bit of work required in downloading alternative AppStores or  APKs, or that the games can simply be played in your phone browser. We'll make sure to detail that for each game, though. Anyway, read on to find a new game or experience to play Off The AppStore.

SPOILERS! This may be one of the few times I must protect your delicate little eyes from the secrets I'm about to reveal. Before we get to that, let's first talk about fans. If you like something, you're a fan. Don't blame me, blame the dictionary, or society if you want an easy target. While some fans can be insufferable constructs of cringe, others get inspired by what they like and make something only they can make. They want to share their passion with us in whatever way they know how. Gatolinie is one such fan (of TWO things, oh my god, so wild) and has brought us their fanfiction in the form of Undertale Vs Gojo.

Let's break it down: Undertale is a pixel indie RPG made by Toby Fox in 2015 that is considered one of the weirdest, most emotional, and best RPGs of all time. Then there's Satoru Gojo, an overpowered Japanese heartthrob from the anime Jujutsu Kaisen. Now, what if the main character from Undertale (Frisk) and Gojo decided to fight? Well, there's a high chance that an entire reality will break into pieces. But it's not that simple… You have to win the fight first.

You play as the version of Frisk who has gone down the path of violence, killing every monster and character they've come across, essentially becoming the villain. After defeating one of the game's hardest bosses, you come across Satoru Gojo, ripped from his universe and dropped into your path. He's in your way, and you decide that the only way through is with violence. Of course, as an anime mentor character, Gojo is exceptionally fast and strong, with a power that literally prevents any attack from touching him. This will be a difficult fight, and Gojo will give you everything he's got.

Undertale Vs Satoru Gojo is a 2D pixel RPG fan game about using Undertale mechanics to fight one of the most popular and powerful anime characters. A lot of effort went into the animations for Gojo, his attacks, and the Undertale UI to blend these two worlds as seamlessly as possible. It's short but challenging, and don't expect to beat it on your first try. You're encouraged to keep going just to talk to Gojo some more, see more of his attacks, and see if you can still come out on top.

Undertale Vs Gojo is available to download and play from its itch.io page!

#4328. Tenebris Somnia Review – A Hair-Raising And Entertaining Throwback

Tenebris Somnia channels the old-school appeal of classic point-and-click adventures, survival horror, and full-motion-video (FMV) experiences, then smartly modernizes them to create a creepy, entertaining experience. Surviving the twisted threats of a demonic dream world is a tightly packed adventure that rewards you with what’s essentially an impressive indie horror film peppered throughout. It’s a nightmare you may not want to wake up from.

The blend of live-action and in-game storytelling works well in Tenebris Somina’s adventure, which begins when protagonist Julia visits the apartment of her filmmaker ex-boyfriend, Ivan, after suffering recurring nightmares of him being massacred by monsters. What begins as a well-meaning check-in on his status spirals down an unsettling rabbit hole when Julia’s worst fears are realized and then some. The dialogue-free tale presents a scary but fascinating exploration of obsession, both in art and in romance, that constantly delivers surprising, and at times upsetting, revelations during its eight-hour runtime. While Tenebris Somnia sometimes leans a little too far into “tell, don’t show” territory when explaining the cool lore of its supernatural threats, I never felt lost or confused about the wild things that regularly unfold on screen.

FMV experiences are nothing new, but Tenebris Somnia’s live-action scenes are a highlight. They’re well shot, sport impressively gruesome practical effects, and even present visual clues that make them important to gameplay. These scenes are additive, never taking too much time away from the in-game action, and they feel well placed to elicit the strongest emotional response. I also appreciate how the live scenes fit thematically, as much of Tenebris Somnia’s tale centers on a horror film shot by Ivan and Julia that significantly impacted their former relationship; at times, it’s like watching a movie about the movie. While I enjoy smaller moments, like opening a door to trigger a live-action jump scare, the filmmaking succeeds in selling Julia's emotions and the cast's reactions. Seeing real fear, concern, and determination in Julia’s eyes as she navigates a dreamworld made up of Ivan’s memories helped endear me to what would otherwise be a featureless pixel sprite.

Gameplay may look unimpressive due to its old-school adventure game presentation, but Tenebris Somnia’s spin on familiar survival-horror mechanics hits the right notes. Taking place entirely within a dreamlike version of a four-story apartment building, you’ll traverse floors collecting and combining objects and deciphering clues to solve well-crafted puzzles. I’m impressed by how well the game’s puzzles make the most of its limited graphical presentation, including clever scenarios involving mirror/screen reflections I won’t spoil, and how consistently creative they are. One devious exercise even utilizes the game’s limited save points as an unexpected resource in a way that changes how you approach your adventure going forward. No matter how strange puzzles become, they are never opaque, requiring just enough out-of-the-box thinking to make me feel smart when I connect the dots.

Battling grotesque monsters (which, naturally, look even creepier in live-action) also feels good, with melee and gunplay sporting deliberate animations reminiscent of classic adventure games without feeling mechanically clunky. Taking on multiple enemies by swinging a pipe or blowing them away with a shotgun feels better than it looks, and the most intense encounters end just as they approach the line of becoming overwhelming.

Boss battles, perhaps most unexpectedly for a largely puzzle-focused adventure, are fun and distinct from each other, be it wave-based bouts against small gremlin-like foes, protecting a fragile effigy of yourself from a parade of demented house servants, or battling literal mirror images of a tentacled flesh monster the Resident Evil series would be proud to claim. Managing limited ammo and health strikes a good balance of feeling tense but not oppressive. Playing conservatively is rewarding, as few non-boss threats need to be engaged if you can evade them well enough. But when I did find myself down to my last bullet or on the verge of death, Tenebris Somnia lets you feel the pinch just long enough before dropping a box of bullets or a health vial at the right moment.

Tenebris Somnia mines the enjoyable nostalgia of playing the horror games of yesteryear without feeling dated in the worst way. Weaving a solid indie horror film adds to the experience rather than feeling like a gimmick. The result is a captivating, well-executed survival-horror romp that maintains a hair-raising atmosphere with a fraction of the pixels of other genre giants.

#4327. PUBG's extraction shooter spin-off, Black Budget, is finally going to be playable next month

The most interesting development in the PUBG universe, PUBG: Black Budget, is almost ready to show itself off to a wider group of players.

You’d be forgiven for not remembering PUBG: Black Budget, the extraction off-shoot of the original battle royale shooter, PUBG. Black Budget has been sort of floating around the internet for months, but Krafton never really committed to revealing core details about the game, or when players will actually get to play it.

This changes today, as the publisher - along with the game’s developer, PUBG Studios, have finally lifted the lid off the upcoming shooter.

Black Budget is described as a “tactical” extraction shooter. Squads of players infiltrate a mysterious island trapped in a time loop. There’s a bit of a STALKER element here with anomalies and various, unpredictable environmental shifts.

Coli, the island in question, hides a research facility that holds secrets and artefacts, which is what players will be attempting to extract. This is very much a PvPvE shooter, though PUBG Studios says the focus will be on exploration and discovery, rather than constant combat.

The game’s first set of closed alpha tests is set for December. The first takes place December 12-14, and another is scheduled for December 19-21. That’s six days across two weeks, with the test only being available on PC. Both sessions will be open to players in North America, Europe, and Asia.

As it usually works with these sorts of tets on Steam, the game’s Steam page has a link where you can request access. If granted, you’ll be able to find the closed alpha in your library and download it when the time comes.

Though this is a closed test, Krafton confirmed that players will be able to capture and livestream their gameplay. In fact, watching content creators might be how you get access, as Black Budget is going to have a Twitch Drops event running alongside those sessions.

When I played Arc Raiders prior to its launch, I likened its tense and uncertain atmosphere to that of the early days of PUBG, so it’s going to be very interesting to see what actual PUBG does with the extraction shooter premise.

So far, it sounds like it’s going to be doing its own thing, leaning more into the adventure side of the subgenre, but we’ll have to see how it all shakes out when the tests start. Indeed, the BR-like constantly shrinking circle sounds like it could be a game-changing twist.

#4325. Dragon boy Durin is the star of the show in Genshin Impact's wintry Luna 3 update, launching in early December

Genshin Impact is getting two new characters and a whole host of new content in Version Luna 3, which arrives in under two weeks.

The latest HoYoverse Special Program has brought us big Genshin Impact news. Version Luna 3 has been fully revealed, continuing the Nod-Krai story. The new chapter arrives December 3 across all platforms.

The Moon-Prayer Night is the big in-world festival, marking Dameselette's final night before she sets off for the moon. The new update, of course, introduces new playable characters, one with an interesting mechanic.

The events of this new chapter take place following Rarcher of Solnari’s defeat. The victory has given way to the Moon-Prayer Night celebrations, which brings various stalls to the Nasha Town, alongside a new souvenir stamp book where you can record your memories.

All is not fine, however, as Alice and Nicole Reeyn come bearing some bad news about phantoms appearing across the Nod-Krai region at Teyvat's borders. There’s a mystery to be uncovered here, and your journey to do so won’t be a lonely one.

The highly-anticipated Durin is at last the new playable character. A 5-Star Pyro Sword wielder, Durin can switch between two different forms: one lets him deal damage, while the other is best suited to supporting the team.

Durin was once a dragon, you see, who was later given a human body. This is why he’s able to switch forms. The more powerful, Abyssal-infused form can launch major attacks on single targets to boost his own Vaporize and Melt damage, while his support form reduces enemies’ Elemental Resistance and deals AoE Pyro damage.

Durin’s Story Quest will shed more light on that aspect of his life, and completing it earns you a reward for him. Speaking of quests, completing the Archon Quest will grant you 500 Primogems. As a member of Hexenzirkel, Durin and other characters can gain new powers when you complete more quests in Moon-Prayer Night.

All characters connected to the Hexenzirkel can benefit from certain story quests tied to their abilities. This is a big new addition, and will affect Venti, Klee, Albedo, Mona, Razor, Fischl, and Sucrose - all of whom can become Hexerei characters. This ties into the new Hexerei Secret Rite effect, which will trigger when two or more Hexerei characters are present. The effect boosts the entire party’s combat effectiveness.

The other new character in Luna 3 is Jahoda, a 4-Star Anemo Bow wielder who’s great at healing teammates and absorbing Elements, which she can then use to deal damage. The first phase of Luna 3 will feature Durin and Jahoda, alongside the return of Venti. The second phase sees no new character debuts, but does feature the return of Varesa and Xilonen.

There’s more to get excited about in Luna 3, even if you don’t feel like spending most of your time in Nod-Krai. The Soulblazers' Snowbound Journey event will take you back to Dragonspine, where you’ll find winter-theme minigames appropriate to an update cycle spanning December to January. This is how you can earn the 4-Star Rainbow Serpent's Rain Bow, too.

Beyond that, you can also look forward to the Miliastra Wonderland UGC module getting new updates. The Wonderland Resource Center is where creators can get and share resources through the editing tool.

#4324. 8 Best Hallway Simulator JRPGs

Usama Mehmood is a Senior Writer at DualShockers with more than five years of experience in the video game industry. He has been writing professionally since 2021 and covering games since 2022, with work spanning guides, lists, reviews, and features across action-adventure games, JRPGs, open-world titles, racing games,

To those unaware, the term “Hallway Sim” for JRPGs was derived from Final Fantasy 13, one of the black sheep of the series. It describes games where exploration takes a backseat to linear level design as you spend most of your time running down narrow corridors, fighting enemies, and watching the occasional cutscene before moving on to the next hallway.

And while that might sound like a recipe for disaster to anyone who enjoys getting lost in sprawling worlds, there’s something oddly comforting about a JRPG that knows exactly where it wants you to go. Of course, FF13 isn't the only game guilty of this design philosophy, nor is it necessarily the worst offender. Many JRPGs have traded sprawling overworlds for a more focused, linear experience, and some are all the better for it if you ask me.

If you love JRPGs but get bogged down by open world activities, check out the these JRPGs for players tired of open world.

So, if you're tired of open-world RPGs that seem to eat up every waking hour of your life, these hallway-simulator JRPGs might be exactly what you need, so why not set the term's derogatory meaning aside for just this once, pretty please?

We’re at the racelines, so I figured we’d open with the Tales of series, a line of games where I’ll gladly rise from my comatose grave to proudly defend Berseria. But see, you’re lucky because we’re talking about Tales of Arise today. What makes Arise stand out as a hallway simulator is how much it accomplishes with a largely linear structure.

The journey with Dahna’s rebellious gang of misfits is filled with a multitude of hub areas across various regions, and although they feature a bit of verticality here and there, the hallway bit quite literally shows up in the final act of the game, as hilarious as that may sound to someone who played it fully.

But hey, at least the real-time combat adds plenty of excitement to these otherwise straightforward maps and progression routes. The game is still an absolute blast to play, so don’t let anyone convince you otherwise, because Alphen and Shionne's budding growth certainly deserve your attention.

Despite its modern-day Tokyo setting, Tokyo Xanadu eX+ is a great example of a hallway simulator JRPG because its world is much more linear than its urban backdrop initially suggests. Don’t get me wrong, the game still has plenty to enjoy in its social-sim aspect that’ll strongly remind you of the Persona series' DNA.

But the cracks start to show once you dive into the actual gameplay, partly because the dungeons are (mostly) long corridors with small rooms in between, packed with enemies, your usual (and basic) environmental puzzles, and a boss waiting at the end. That doesn't make Tokyo Xanadu eX+ a bad JRPG, though, but I can see the repetition setting in for anyone else when the game railroads you along on this high-school high-jinks adventure.

Now, I know Soul Hackers 2 got a hefty amount of slack upon release and well past the honeymoon period, to the point where it had a divided audience, but hey, at least I’m in the minority who loved what I've played so far. However, I’d be lying to you if I didn’t admit that its actual world exploration feels surprisingly restrictive. All the way down to the dungeon design.

And the biggest offender is its Soul Matrix, where almost every character-specific dungeon is essentially a collection of long, repetitive corridors with branching paths that occasionally lead to treasure chests, enemies, or locked doors.

Even the main story dungeons aren't particularly special; if I’m being blunt, they often feel more like elaborate indoor mazes than places you'd genuinely want to explore, which is unfortunate because, aside from that, Soul Hackers 2 is a very decent JRPG if given the proper time and attention, with an adoring cast of characters at the helm.

Not every JRPG received the spotlight it deserved, as demonstrated by these obscure games from famous developers.

I’ll admit up front here: the Wild Arms series has a serious cult following. The first three games gave you these sprawling overworlds, goofy puzzle dungeons, and a Wild West-meets-fantasy vibe that nothing else quite matched. Then Wild Arms 4 came along and decided the best way to tell a story was to put you in a corridor… and keep you there.

Oh right, it does have one thing doing a bit of the heavy lifting: the hex-grid battle system. It’s a genuinely interesting twist on the combat system of other JRPGs at that time and keeps regular fights from feeling like standard menu-fests. But even that can’t fully hide how little there is to do between battles, since the game largely funnels you from one encounter to the next, with little opportunity to wander off the beaten path.

Scarlet Nexus has one of the coolest combat systems I’ve played in an action RPG; quite underrated if you ask me, but I have to be honest: you spend most of your time walking down corridors for the gameplay portion at least. And by the time you reach the endgame, it honestly feels like one long walk between fights every single time.

Don’t get me wrong; it’s a pretty good game, but it's built almost entirely out of hallways, and every main mission follows the same pattern. You push forward through a narrow, linear path, hit a small arena where a few Others drop in, and clear it out with your melee might and psychokinesis (PK).

The Brain Map and Bond Episodes add some welcome character progression and downtime, but they don't change the fact that Scarlet Nexus is a remarkably linear experience. But hey, as long as you try both of its two main characters’ routes, I promise Scarlet Nexus will be worth your time and investment, given how much dumb fun it offers.

I thought we’d dabble into the retro scene and talk about Grandia 2, one of the most beloved JRPGs on the Dreamcast. The combat is some of the best the genre has ever produced, and Ryudo is a genuinely fun protagonist, a grumpy mercenary who’d rather be anywhere else. But if you ask me what the game feels like from hour to hour, I’d say it’s like walking through a very pretty, very long hallway with a really good fight system attached.

Let’s talk about the dungeons because the game is built almost entirely out of narrow, winding paths that lead from Point A to Point B, with the occasional fork that gives you a treasure chest as a consolation prize for turning left. And to be fair, this is a very common JRPG design philosophy, especially from that era, since plenty of games from that generation are built around a story-first, linear structure.

In the most complimentary way I can put it, Grandia 2 is a hallway simulator with a killer combat system, a charming cast, and one of the most memorable villains of its time, but… just don’t go in expecting a world to explore.

I might be bending the rules here, but forgive me because I needed a way to compartmentalize this list without having one less entry. But hey, I guess that means this is a safe space to rave about Stranger of Paradise. Let’s get one thing straight, obviously. This is technically a loot-driven action RPG with a job system, which is about as JRPG as it gets, but the world barely exists, so there’s no cozy little town for you to wander, no overworld to explore, no little NPCs telling you about their lost cat or dad that ran out to get groceries.

Instead, you pick a mission from a menu, stare at a loading screen, and get tossed into a hallway-esque dungeon. Not that it’s a killing point, because this is, on all fronts, another fantastic Team Ninja game that gives you plenty of build options to take down its trash-fodder foes and hard-hitting boss fights. And if you’ve got the complete edition, the DLCs are a worthwhile plus for anyone who wants second helpings out of the game’s combat system.

As much as I’d want to make you roll your eyes by going with FF13, I decided the less obvious top pick to sign off with here would be Final Fantasy VII Remake. With Revelation coming in the first half of 2027, it just felt right.

The first part of this remake trilogy takes the opening few hours of the original, the bit in Midgar that you used to blow through in an afternoon, and turns it into a full-length game. That’s an ambitious swing, but despite what some of the divided fanbase may tell you, it works splendidly to give its charming cast of characters a whole new sense of direction and relationship-building moments.

What's particularly noticeable is the contrast between Midgar's enormous scale and how little of it you're actually allowed to explore. Even when the game introduces side quests and optional activities in areas like the Sector 7 Slums or Wall Market, these locations are relatively small hubs connected by straightforward routes, not fully explorable districts.

It’s not a true hallway-sim JRPG, as the term suggests for its sister game in the series, but these corridor-esque maps leave little room for meaningful exploration or player-driven detours. Again, not a diss at the game since it’s a lovely time for both hardcore fans and newcomers.

If you're lacking in time or energy for long games, try one of these JRPGs for Players Tired of 100-Hour Time Commitments.

#4323. A Mass Effect 5 Trailer Featuring Liara Appears To Have Leaked Following BioWare's Closure

In case you missed the tragic news yesterday, EA laid off 400 employees this week, including all of BioWare. The studio behind Mass Effect, Dragon Age, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, and more, has been shut down, and its last remaining project was canceled. The game in question was a fifth entry in the Mass Effect universe, and BioWare shared very little about it – not even an official name. Following the studio's closure, however, a trailer for the sci-fi sequel started circulating around the internet.

While no official BioWare representatives have confirmed that the footage is real, Bloomberg reporter Jason Schreier claims that it is. Schreier has a history of credible reporting in the field, and was the first to break the news about the layoffs. IGN has also stated that it confirmed the trailer's legitimacy.

If you want to see for yourself, you can watch the trailer on Reddit.

"The following is in-engine footage form our small team," text at the start of the video reads. "It uses our pre-production assets." The footage shows no gameplay, but includes a good-looking CG cutscene of a new protagonist speaking with an asari woman in a crowded bar. As he tells her about his life, we see glimpses of him as a soldier, then as some kind of spy, traveling to several planets to track down conflicts and "stopping them before they start." After the asari woman reveals that she's been "starting the fires" he's trying to prevent, another woman behind her lowers a hood. This new woman reveals herself as Liara T'Soni, one of Mass Effect's most iconic characters.

Then, Liara and the protagonist team up to take out the woman at the bar and her henchmen, using guns and telekinetic abilities. The trailer fades to black, then fades back in to reveal the game's would-be title: Mass Effect Universe. It's a great-looking trailer – it's a shame the game will never see the light of day.

If you want to join us in grieving BioWare, we republished an oral history of the studio that was originally written by former editor Matt Bertz in 2016. You can also read our cover stories on BioWare's most recent releases: Dragon Age: The Veilguard, Mass Effect: Legendary Edition, Anthem, and Mass Effect Andromeda.

#4321. Battlefield 6 kicks off its first free trial post the Black Ops 7 launch to twist that knife

Activision has done its own fair share of Battlefield 6 counterprogramming prior to that game's release, and EA is here to repay the favour with Black Ops 7.

Even if you don’t care about the rivalries between the top multiplayer first-person shooters series, it’s hard to ignore how much EA wanted to stick it to Call of Duty this year with Battlefield 6.

Activision saw that coming early enough that it ran multiple free weekends around major moments for EA’s game, including its launch, seemingly in an effort to capture some of those players and keep them away from BF6.

Both Battlefield 6, and Black Ops 7 have now launched, and though exact sales figures may never be detrmined (though EA did announce 7 million sold in the first week), it’s very clear at this point from every metric we can see that BF6 came out on top this year.

The recent Black Ops 7 launch clearly hasn’t made many people happy, so just like Activision made Black Ops 6 free to play at BF6’s launch, EA has now done the same with its own game. The Battlefield 6 free trial, which was announced last week, is just an hour away at the time of this writing.

This is the first trial for the core game, and it arrives some six weeks after Battlefield 6 officialy launched, and four weeks following the release of the free-to-play Battlefield Redsec, which has battle royale and other components.

Beyond all the drama surrounding the two rival shooter franchises, the Battlefield 6 trial is itself pretty straightfoward, and is notably nowhere near as genrous as some of the Call of Duty ones we’ve seen recently.

The trial goes live today at 4am PT, 7am ET, 12pm GMT across all platforms, and will be available for a week; ending Tuesday, December 2. It includes three core maps: Siege of Cairo, Eastwood, and Blackwell Fields.

Players will have access to four game modes, played on different versions of the same maps. Conquest, Breakthrough, Sabotage, and Team Deathmatch will all be available to choose from, and there don’t appear to be any level or XP limits in the trial.

Unfortunatley, just as the free trial was about to go live, the game got hit with a major matchmaking outage that took down all matchmaking in the core game, leaving Redsec unaffected.

Hopefully EA can resolve this issue before the trial officially kicks off.

#4319. Wuthering Waves and the Constant Pursuit of Improving the Player Experience

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

This article was produced in collaboration with our sponsor, Kuro Games.

Live service games rely on two major factors to stay afloat: constant content and community satisfaction. These aims sound perfectly aligned. After all, players want more things to do in their favorite games, so just giving them more should do it all, right? Easier said than done, especially when improper quality control can doom a game rapidly, especially in the eyes of new players.

Leaking in a similar vein to Persona 3 Reload, footage showcasing a Persona 1 Remake has appeared, looking almost too good to be true.

This Article was made with help from our sponsor, Kuro Games. Wuthering Waves is a game that teetered on that brink, fumbling its first impression with early execution that left much to be desired across various levels, prompting a period of deep reflection and iteration. Despite this slow start, I'd put WuWa right alongside No Man's Sky on the pedestal of "Most Improved Games from Launch", largely thanks to Kuro Games' willingness to respond to community grievances with actual, tangible change.

From gameplay overhauls, massively improved visual presentation, to a heavily expanded story that feels like it's just now hitting a second wind, Wuthering Waves is a refreshing example of just how far a team with open communication and pure passion can push a product toward excellence, allowing WuWa to stand alongside titans in their genre’s sphere.

As we approach 3.8, it's really wild to look back on just how rough WuWa's initial launch was, rife with complaints about an overall experience that still needed polish. Yet, its remarkable combat already displayed the clear potential of a standout game, and Kuro was quick to show just how much things were willing to change.

As early as 1.3, the plot was starting to roll, giving early adopters a real incentive to keep coming back with each update, even as bugs were constantly being ironed out. Kuro has been great about acknowledging and squashing these bugs.

Even this early, you can see how Kuro was improving not only the gameplay feel, but the character presentation. 1.0 WuWa still had room for growth in character writing, a flaw that has been so rewarding to see them improve on patch after patch. This progress is another grand showcase of Kuro's resilience and unwavering commitment to quality.

Despite this willingness to shake things up, WuWa never forsook the genuinely interesting parts of its world that caught the community's attention all those years ago. Instead, Kuro built on to what worked, shown in 2.0's sweeping set of improvements.

2.0 felt like WuWa's Realm Reborn moment, combining all the early community critiques of the presentation, exploration, and story into a proper grand reintroduction. With new features like flight, old pain points when it came to grinding and map clearing were easy to handle, all while feeling like a proper reward.

After the departures of various leading developers, PlatinumGames wants fans of Bayonetta to know they aren't through with the Umbra Witch.

While other open-world games generally have players explore their maps on foot, WuWa is constantly improving the exploration experience with new vehicles, methods of traversal, and tricks to keep the world exciting. Solaris-3 always feels like it's getting bigger, reminding players that WuWa is a proper sci-fi setting, with this distinctive blend of sci-fi identity and exploration being one of the reasons it continues to draw me in.

The Wuthering Waves community itself is more than willing to chirp up about issues. Kuro Games, in turn, respects and takes player feedback seriously, maintaining an open and proactive dialogue with the community.

Despite this slow start, I'd put WuWa right alongside No Man's Sky on the pedestal of "Most Improved Games from Launch", largely thanks to Kuro Games' willingness to respond to community grievances with actual, tangible change.

The studio isn't without fault, as the game's rough launch showed, but Kuro makes it easy to sit in their corner when they're so willing to fuse their vision for the game with the community's genuine grievances. The game's longest-running pain point, its lack of early character implementation, is already on the way out. Fan-favorite characters such as Aemeath shows just how far the team has come, with both its storytelling and character writing now reaching an exceptionally high standard. We might be seeing an all-time story for new players post 4.0.

WuWa has more than lived up to my top expectation for games in the genre: a strong protagonist. Watching a MC actually improve and change over the course of the story is so nice to properly see, and Rover's journey from 1.0 to now is genuinely some of the best in the genre.

If you like Action RPGs and other similar titles have burnt you by stonewalling devs or flatlining content, Wuthering Waves is the best recommendation I can possibly give. Constant, open communication, a real active fanbase, and a game created with mountains of love, WuWa really is the full package.

If you're a new or returning player, make sure to check out the official Wuthering Waves page for updates, dev blogs, and upcoming news for the game as a whole. Major title updates are the best time to join, and the current story arc is entering its climactic finale, so don't wait!

#4318. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Review - Silver Bullet

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 arrives at a crossroads for the series, thanks in large part to the inconsistent quality of recent entries. With a shaky predecessor, Infinity Ward had a lot to repair and conclude, especially with 4 set to bookend the rebooted Modern Warfare series. Fortunately, backed up by a fun campaign, thrilling multiplayer, and loads of new modes and content, Modern Warfare 4 makes up for the past and then some.

Modern Warfare 4 continues after the events of 2023’s Modern Warfare 3, with Captain Price hellbent on stopping Makarov and his higher-ups. The story features shifting perspectives, from a new group of ragtag Korean soldiers to familiar characters like Gaz. The character dynamics harken back to the original trilogy, especially in the boots-on-the-ground missions with the South Korean unit, led by Park (played by Beef actor Young Mazino).

For a series that, at least recently, has been more spectacle than story, giving the stakes the time they deserve is nice. While it moves away from the stealthy and modernized elements, it makes sense for the matters at hand. The majority of Modern Warfare 4’s attempts at wrapping up the overarching plot of the rebooted series works, but it rushes through some character arcs and story beats in uneven fashion. Furthermore, much of the game’s cast, especially Mads Mikkelson’s Archer and Prisca Kim’s Ri Ju-Young, are underutilized, which is a shame since they both deliver great performances.

Despite the shortcomings of the campaign, Call of Duty's bread and butter, multiplayer, still delivers. While it doesn’t have the fluidity of Black Ops’ newer entries, the customization and design of weapons and maps make it worth digging into. From small, intimate shooting galleries with Mumbai and Nautical to wide free-for-alls like Coal and Reactor U92, the range helps maintain excitement, even if it gets repetitive over time.

The variety of multiplayer modes keeps things fresh on the battlefield. Returning modes like standard Team Deathmatch and Kill Confirmed continue that enjoyable competitive flair that made them the stars that they are. However, new modes like Combat Outpost and Hijack fit right into the already great lineup. In particular, Combat Outpost upscales your typical 6v6 player count to 24v24, leading to more action and teamwork. Hanging onto a team’s tank, shooting enemies from afar, and taking back outposts is exhilarating, even if it can all go bad moments later by a well-placed RPG shot.

Even after hours of gameplay, the variety of options to craft your perfect gun is impressive. Figuring out the best scope, ammo, stock, and muzzle, as well as the advantages and disadvantages of them, is a fun way of customizing your playstyle. Gunny, a mechanic that helps optimize your gun for certain styles, can help with decision paralysis, but I rarely used it. Not many FPSs go that far and Modern Warfare 4’s commitment to the feature makes it stand out.

The newest mode, DMZ, impresses out of the gate. After a few flat attempts in the past, this is the definitive Call of Duty extraction shooter, whether you play solo, or in duos or trios. Immediately, you’re thrust into the wide open world of Hajin and left to fend for yourselves with what you have and what you can gather and extract. Fans of Arc Raiders and Marathon should feel right at home as the gameplay borrows from the typical extraction shooter experience. Intense, action-packed moments keep you coming back after every win or loss. And the excellent gunplay and level design elevate it into something worthwhile, no matter how you play.

Despite not encountering many live players during my time in Hajin in DMZ, it still proves challenging, even for seasoned pros. The world is not your friend, and taking risks can come at a high cost. A good team, as well as a thoughtful loadout and traits, are required to survive. The unpredictability of it all keeps you on your toes, making for an exciting addition to the already strong multiplayer suite.

Regardless of the mode, Modern Warfare 4 is one of the best-looking Call of Duty titles to date. New York and Paris are lifelike, and it truly embodies the realistic, modern aesthetic the series has always aimed to achieve. However, I encountered a few technical hiccups, especially in the campaign. Slow framerate plagues some high-octane scenes and texture loading is frequent across the board. These distractions are far from game-breaking, but enough to be noticeable.

While the plot execution is a bit shaky, engaging multiplayer options, including DMZ, aptly demonstrate that Infinity Ward can still deliver compelling military-FPS experiences. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is a strong return to form that serves as a solid sendoff for the rebooted subseries.

#4316. The latest Arc Raiders patch is almost entirely about fixing exploits, including all the clipping through locked rooms business

Embark is clearly sick of Arc Raiders players exploiting the game's mechanics to push each other around, and clip through doors and walls.

A fresh Arc Raiders patch has arrived, bringing a host of new fixes to several exploits players have recently been relying on to do things they’re not supposed to, and bypass certain mechanics to get into areas without having to go through proper channels.

The patch is fairly small, and surprisingly doesn’t include any buffs or nerfs to anything in particular.

The list of notes for update 1.4.0 is compact, with a clear focus on addressing several exploits. The biggest one, of course, is the addition of “exploit mitigation mechanisms” to stop players from glitching through locked doors.

This fix applies to all maps, and it’s intended to address an issue whereby players would not bring the required keys to access those areas of the various maps. Locked rooms, if they can be unlocked, often hide a wealth of high-tier and rare loot.

But players have also been using similar exploits to clip through walls and access areas outside the playspace, allowing them to ambush enemy players and set up traps that would be impossible for others to detect.

The game’s recent patch, which was released exactly one week ago, mainly consisted of balance tweaks to some of the more popular weapons and mines. However, it also introduced a few fixes to prevent players from clipping through walls by using barricades.

While on the subject of being in places where you’re not supposed to, the patch blocked exterior access to the locked room inside Spaceport's Control Tower, making it only accessible from inside the tower.

#4313. Amazon’s Mass Effect TV Series Is Reportedly Still In Production Despite BioWare Closure

EA shut down legendary RPG developer BioWare this week, canceling its in-development fifth Mass Effect game as a result. Despite the closure, Amazon Prime’s upcoming Mass Effect streaming series will proceed as planned, according to a report by IGN.

Amazon MGM Studios began developing a Mass Effect series in 2024. At the time, Mass Effect series executive producer Mike Gamble confirmed the show isn't a retelling of the video games, saying, “The show will explore a brand-new story within the universe's timeline, and will be set after the original trilogy. It won't be a retread of Commander Shepard's story – because after all... that's YOUR story, isn’t it?”

With BioWare’s closure, one would think the series would go up in smoke, but sources within Prime Video speaking to IGN confirmed that it remains in development. Furthermore, all of the creatives involved remain so. This includes showrunners Doug Jung (The Cloverfield Paradox, Star Trek Beyond) and Daniel Casey (F9: The Fast Saga, Wardriver), former Marvel Studios head Avi Arad, and Jessica Jones executive producer Karim Zreik. Mike Gamble was also involved, and this report suggests he still is, but it remains to be seen how his position on the project has changed with BioWare’s demise, given he served as a guiding voice from the studio. The Mass Effect series has no release window.

The Mass Effect series joins other video game adaptations Amazon has in the works, which include a third season of Fallout (with Aaron Paul joining the cast), a live-action God of War series starring Dave Bautista, a live-action Tomb Raider series starring Sophie Turner, as well as series based on Life is Strange and Wolfenstein.

For more on Mass Effect, check out our review of the Legendary Edition and our recently republished Oral History of BioWare from 2016.

#4312. Battlefield Labs is coming back for a short session to test out next week's Battlefield 6 update, and you can expect more tests in the future, too

Battlefield Labs is evolving, as it reopens its doors for its next - unusual - session.

Battlefield Studios is seemingly trying something different with Battlefield 6’s next patch, which everyone assumed would be a standard, mid-season update not intended to change the game significantly.

However, it appears that it may bring more to the game than we realised, enough that the developer sees it as an excuse to bring back the pre-launch Battlefield Labs testing initiative.

The December 9 patch kicks off the final phase of the game’s first season, which is set to take the game through the holidays and into the new year. We’ve known about its content for a while, and it’s definitely the lightest, compared to the two previous phases.

Battlefield Studios announced a host of new changes that will be included in the same patch, which are apparently significant enough to require player testing. The developer is reviving Battlefield Labs to help it do so, but only for three two-hour sessions, split across the game’s three main server regions (EU, NA, APAC).

All tests are scheduled for today, December 2, and they remain under NDA. Battlefield Labs is also sticking with PC as its chosen platform yet again, though you will be able to join through Steam this time, alongside the EA app.

The focus of the test will be on three key areas that the December 9 patch will be touching. First, there’s footstep audio, an issue that was really brought into focus with the launch of Redsec Battle Royale. You can expect to hear enemy footsteps from farther away, and intuitively know the type of surface they’re moving on.

The patch also brings another pass to hit registration and netcode, which BF Studios says should improve responsiveness in close-quarter situations. Finally, there are broader changes to other combat areas that the announcement didn’t elaborate on.

All testing will take place on Eastwood, and Operation Firestorm, rotating between Conquest, and Escalation.

Going forward, Battlefield Studios said to expect Labs to be open to more players, and for the process itself to be smoother. The developer wants to have faster turnaround times, after all, so that the initiative can test smaller changes and be more responsive to player feedback.

Some of the more involved, future sessions will include experiments with map layout changes and various other non-standard compositions of player and vehicle numbers. Of course, you can also expect new maps and modes to be tested in Labs, similar to how the CTE was used in Battlefield 4’s long life.

#4310. Remedy Explains Control Resonant's Most Memorable, Unexpected Sequence And Its [REDACTED] Inspirations

Please allow the first sentence here to warn you that this interview discusses a portion of Control Resonant that takes place near the end of the game and is arguably the most unexpected and surprising sequence. I encourage you to experience it without spoilers. So if you haven't beaten the game yet, please do, and then come back to this page.However, if you have beaten the game, or curiosity has driven you to learn what game has been redacted from the headline and why (it's the 1995 Super Nintendo RPG, EarthBound, by the way), then please read on.

In the late-game of Control Resonant – basically right before you tackle the final confrontation – the game suddenly shifts timeframe and genre to become a 16-bit RPG. The nostalgic lens turns the game into something that feels like 1995's EarthBound, complete with turn-based battles, in order to explain the trauma that Jesse and Dylan went through at a young age after they came across an object of power: the slide projector. The whole sequence is funny, heartbreaking, weird, and importantly effective at making you feel you are seeing a part of their past. It was particularly effective on me as I have fond memories of playing EarthBound and games like it when I was young. To see and experience Dylan and Jesse's childhood this way felt accurate, as absurd as that sounds.

I reached out to Remedy to specifically discuss that portion of the game. You can find the full e-mail interview below with the team members who contributed to its creation.

The big RPG backstory sequence for Jesse and Dylan – why approach the storytelling that way?

Lead level designer, Anne-Marie Grönroos: The basis for the whole sequence is that the Hedron attacks Dylan's mind, breaks his reality apart, and he has to rebuild himself. We wanted the reality-breaking part to affect the game itself and have the player feel some of the confusion Dylan is feeling by breaking the fourth wall.

Who pitched that sequence, how did they pitch it, and was it difficult to sell to the larger team?

Grönroos: At Remedy, ideas rarely come from a single person or team, and we rarely do formal pitches, but rather discuss and workshop ideas cross-craft until they start taking the shape of something we like. The initial idea from the writer was for this to be a text-based adventure, to return to a very early form of a video game to show that the Patterning is devolving him, but an Alan Wake 2 DLC had already done that, and we wanted to find something else.

Independently, some months ago a level designer had suggested a sidequest with JRPG pixel graphics, but that had gone nowhere. I remembered that and suggested doing an old Final Fantasy-style JRPG here, which also felt more fitting since that’s the type of game Dylan and Jesse would have played in their childhood, and not a text-based adventure. People got excited about that, and after some concerns about feasibility, we went forth with it. It helped that the level designer who had originally wanted to do the JRPG side quest is a big fan of these types of games and has made them before. I wouldn’t have dropped something this crazy on someone who wasn’t passionate about it and ready to figure out how to do it with our engine that’s not built for anything like this.

Is EarthBound (Mother in Japan) the primary inspiration for that sequence? Are there big fans of those games at Remedy?

Senior level designer in charge of the JRPG quest, Arhi Makkonen:The whole Quest was born from that childhood feeling I had when playing old JRPGs – Final Fantasy, Breath of Fire, Chrono Trigger, Secret of Mana, Bahamut Lagoon, and yes, Mother. The most important thing for me was capturing that feeling of a time when games felt like magic. I think many people can relate to that nostalgia, and now Jesse and Dylan share that feeling in the game.Visually, Mother was a major inspiration of course. Juuso Anttila is the concept artist who did all the splendid pixel art for Rebuild quest. Mother's style fits the mysterious Americana small town vibe perfectly. We also couldn't pass up the pun about a story revolving around "Not-Mother" that was made in the style of Mother.

Was it difficult to implement the sequence into the game? Did Remedy's Northlight Engine need significant work to account for the sequence?

Makkonen: The Northlight engine was designed to work perfectly for third-person action games. Well, Rebuild Quest is pretty much the opposite of that. Northlight is a specialized tool rather than a general-purpose one, so we had to come up with some rather creative solutions to create a 2D JRPG.

First of all, we’re faking the 2D look. In reality, the entire JRPG Ordinary exists within a 3D world that the camera simply views from directly overhead. It occupies a tiny patch in a remote corner of the game world—a space where 3D Dylan would barely have room to stand. The entire game-within-a-game is written in Lua; our incredibly versatile game designer, Tommi Saalasti, created the underlying system, upon which I was then able to build the story.

Since we didn't really have the tools to create a game like this, I had to hand-code every single detail. Dylan takes one step up, Dylan turns left (where Jesse hopefully is at that moment), text box 1, text box 2. The Lua script for the Rebuild quest alone probably contains as many lines of code as all the other quests in the game combined. And then there were things like animations were restricted to a maximum of two frames, and some UI elements were created using static particle effects.

So yes, we faced all sorts of challenges and compromises, but at the heart of it all was a wonderful story – simply told in a somewhat unconventional way. We trusted that the narrative would make up for some of the imperfections.

Remedy has a reputation for big unexpected and often crazy singular moments. What are the conversations like around delivering those? In pre-production, are there conversations like, "What is the big moment for this one?" Or do they happen pretty naturally?

Grönroos: They both happen naturally and we also have conversations about what the big moments should be. Sometimes we like a section so much that we decide to put even more resources and importance to it, even if it wasn’t supposed to be all that important from the get-go. The Into the Sinkhole quest, for instance, is a quest that wasn’t planned to be a “tentpole moment” from the start, but we kept putting more effort into it when it was shaping up to be something very special.

But most setpieces in the game were planned to be such from the early stages of pre-production. In Resonant, we wanted to have multiple standout moments instead of a single sequence like the Ashtray Maze overshadowing everything else, and I’m happy to see that players have different favorites.

And a different approach from Control is that several of these memorable moments (Sinkhole, Underpass Fault, the JRPG section) are more emotional and subdued instead of bombastic action (although we also have big action setpieces), which was an interesting challenge itself.

Was there a fear that the visuals would limit the emotional impact of the sequence?

Grönroos: Yes, but we decided to trust the writing. Several other games have managed to deliver a similar emotional impact despite pixel graphics (and sometimes because of them, since the level [of] abstraction can make characters more relatable and up to the player’s interpretation), so we weren’t too concerned.

Was there a fear that action game fans would be frustrated by the RPG sequence?

Grönroos: Yes, this was the main concern about the sequence. It was a very polarizing sequence in the playtests: people either loved or hated it. We did discuss shortening it significantly, but in the end decided to keep it as it is but added some fast travel options and make some parts skippable. There were more fans than haters, and we didn’t want to sacrifice something we really enjoyed.

How concerned were you about the actual RPG mechanics of that sequence?

Makkonen: Since Rebuild doesn't feature a vast number of battles, we didn't need to build particularly deep RPG or progression systems. The combat served as an additional storytelling tool – illustrating how bullies torment Dylan, showing his first fight (against rats, naturally), and depicting his eventual abduction by the FBC.

Refining the combat to be simple, yet offer the player meaningful choices required a few iterations. In addition to standard attacks, the children can occasionally use special abilities: Dylan delivers a heavy blow to a single enemy, while Jesse fires at everyone. Enemies deal enough damage that defending becomes necessary when multiple foes target the same character.

The lightbulbs in The Underpass mission goes in similarly unexpected, animated directions. How did that mission come about? What was the pitch like for that one?

Grönroos: That one started with the idea of doing something comically mundane, switching lightbulbs, and adding a paranatural twist to it. The cartoon man wasn’t in the initial version, but instead we were going to do live action videos and have Dylan get stuck in that video as the end twist. They were supposed to be old-fashioned “work safety” videos explaining how to change lightbulbs, and as the quest went on, it became more and more obvious that the maintenance guy in the videos was too aware of what Dylan was doing. This all came out from a one-hour workshop.

There wasn’t really a pitch, but rather a back-and-forth like “could we do a quest about Dylan changing lightbulbs in a ritualistic way? We could have these sentient work safety videos explain how to do it and “Dylan could get trapped inside the video.” Much later, when the live action turned out to be a no-go, we pivoted to the current cartoon instead, and that was even funnier than our initial idea.

To read Game Informer's review of Control Resonant, follow the link.

#4309. Honkai: Star Rail 3.8 will run for an extra two weeks while Version 4.0 is in the oven

The next Honkai: Star Rail update is upon us, and there's a mix of good - and unusual news.

HoYoverse just hosted a sizeable Honkai: Star Rail Special Program, revealing more than just the game’s next major update. Version 3.8 was the big highlight, of course, with the new release arriving soon, on December 16-17 depending on your server region.

Alongside showing everything coming with this next update, the developer also announced that 3.8 will go on for eight weeks, rather than the usual six. V3.8 is dubbed "Memories are the Prelude to Dreams", and it brings an end to the Amphoreus journey.

The story in "Memories are the Prelude to Dreams" takes place after the final battle of Amphoreus, where Constance "The Dahlia" appears to deliver a twist: the Trailblazer's memories are scattered, with many parts missing.

This final quest revolves around finding them in order to piece together the mystery, and involves a return to Penacony. This memory-hunting adventure is told from the perspective of Firefly, which will also explain how she entered the dreamscape initially and met the squad.

The new playable character is The Dahlia, whose power is linked to the the Remembrance path, which allows her to fabricate memories. Despite taking her powers from the Remembrance, The Dhalia actually follows the Path of Nihility in-game: she’s a 5-Star character who shines in teams dealing Break DMG.

The Dhalia can unleash a Gloomy Zone that causes Toughness Reduction inflicted by allies to trigger Super Break DMG, even before you break your enemies’ Weaknesses. The Dahlia can also invite one teammate to become her Dance Partner, which allows them (and her) to deal additional Super Break DMG each time they attack an enemy. If you trigger her Ultimate after picking a Dance Partner, she applies Type Weaknesses of both partners to enemies.

While The Dahlia is the only new character appearing in this final Amphoreus update, there'll be reruns aplenty, with an unusual third banner phase to make up for the extra long wait for 4.0. Appropriately for her role in the story, Firefly will make her return alongside The Dahlia in Phase 1, while Fugue and Lingsha will both have banner reruns in Phase 2, which is expected on January 7th. A bonus two-week-long Phase 3 will then begin on January 28th, seeing brief reappearances for popular returning characters Aglaea and Sunday, before things (presumably) go back to normal with the new annual update.

Something else to look forward to in 3.8 is The Chrysos Awoo Championship, which invites players to become chimera trainers and compete in team-based battles. The Remnants of Twilight event kicks off with the new patch, too, featuring its own set of challenges. However, HoYoverse have confirmed that there won't be an extra event during Phase 3 — but hopefully that'll give you some time to wrap up the last of the Amphoreus story content, which is longer than the previous four chapters put together.
