#4308. Nearly 3 in 4 Gamers Are More Likely to Wait for Sales, Newzoo and G2A Find

A Montreal-based Game enthusiast who has been writing about the industry since 2013.

Price and gaming has taken on an entirely new meaning over the last year. The idea of waiting for a sale became a borderline meme over a decade ago, when Steam started running infamous deep-discount sales on digital games. A cursory search for “Gabe” or “Steam Sale” can be a long timetraveling road through years of in-jokes from the enthusiast community. These goofs and gags barely hold up all these years later, but they do harken back to a simpler time in the world of games pricing.

Today, conversations around discounts, sales, and pricing will launch just about anyone from the wide-world of gaming into a tirade about a whole host of criticism of the game industry: what do we do about physical games, do we even own digital games, is Mario Kart World worth X number of dollars. The list goes on. In the market of 2026, between the cost of individual games, the increasing price of hardware, live-service games, and monthly subscriptions, there are more factors than ever that influence player spending habits. It’s a fascinating time to look into how pricing dynamics are influencing the industry.

A report from Newzoo and G2A.COM found that 73% of surveyed players say they are more likely to wait for sales these days. The survey included 6,166 active PC or console players aged 18–55 across six countries, all of whom had purchased or played at least one AAA or AA game in the previous year. The study, “Game purchasing behavior in an era of choice” investigates how modern PC and console players are choosing to spend their hard-earned money in 2026. And while, yes, most players are happy to let the release date come and go so they can get a good deal on a given game, that doesn’t mean that players are entirely content to wait particularly long for a discount.

Wardogs lead developer Joe Brammer took to X (formerly Twitter) to offer another perspective on why studios are struggling to stay afloat.

Looking back at their purchases over the past three years, respondents reported buying just 42% of games before or during release month: 17% through pre-orders and 25% during the month itself. So how does this break down outside of the launch window?

In summary, of the purchases respondents recalled making over the past three years, 82% happened before release or within a game’s first year, including pre-orders. The remaining 18% happened more than a year after release. Crucially, it’s worth bearing in mind that this describes the timing of reported purchases. Still, it highlights how important it is for publishers keep a game top-of-mind after launch, and make sure players are able to take advantage of discounts and other offers post-launch.

Among players who buy beyond release month, the average expected wait for a discount worth considering is 4.9 months. And naturally, how deep the discount cuts plays a big role in purchasing behaviour.

On average, respondents consider a game reasonably priced at 29% off, and Newzoo notes that a 45% discount represents a ‘good deal.’ In their sample, audiences considered a 70% cut a potential red flag to a game’s quality, which is an interesting note that’s hard to unsee when you browse Steam.

Now's your chance to save 50% on one of the best releases of the summer.

One of the other notable data points from the study is that despite players being happy to wait for discounts, they also consider games a very high-value medium. In fact, 69% consider it better value than entertainment such as television, films and music, while 62% agree that game prices reflect rising development costs and complexity. Of course, that doesn’t mean audiences aren’t always still looking for a deal if they can take advantage of one.

“With nearly 60% of purchases occurring later than release month, publishers need long-term monetisation strategies that go well beyond the first week or month,” Newzoo research director Alexis Pamboris said in the press release.

Where people shop is another piece of the puzzle. Official digital storefronts (PSN, Steam, etc.) are expectedly dominant, but 24% of subjects in the study claim to use third-party marketplaces to purchase or research a title. G2A, which co-authored the report and runs its own marketplace, states that the alternate purchasing channels give players more choice. As stated by G2A chief business officer Katarzyna Jakubiec, “different purchasing channels serve different consumer needs.”

Most players, especially those with a Steam backlog, can probably relate to some of Newzoo and G2A’s findings. Waiting for a sale is a familiar part of deciding what to buy, from a box of cereal to a piping-hot copy of Grand Theft Auto VI. What’s interesting is how clearly that patience shows up in the numbers. Players still want new games, but many are willing to let release day pass until the price feels right. For publishers, the challenge is giving them a reason to finally move something from the wishlist to the library.

For a full deep-dive on all that findings inside Newzoo and G2A's report, you can visit their site here.

#4306. Tomorrow’s Battlefield 6 patch is the first step towards improving footstep audio, and it might actually fix the settings reset bug

The next major Battlefield 6 patch is nearly upon us, and Battlefield Studios is promising a bounty of changes - including a couple of fixes to some big bugs.

Battlefield 6 is about to receive a new update. Version 1.1.3.0 is set to arrive tomorrow, December 9 to kick off the third and final phase of the game’s first season. Winter Offensive brings some holiday-themed new content to the game, but it’s not the most interesting part of the patch.

That honour goes to a couple of the high-level changes Battlefield Studios has included with the new patch, which range from a major pass on audio to a fix for a particularly annoying bug that’s been seemingly introduced with a recent patch.

Thew new content takes the form of a limited-time version of the game’s Empire State map, which covers it in snow and tweaks its layout slightly. To go along with that there are new limited-time modes for both multiplayer and Redsec’s Gauntlet. The event mode will be available in Conquest, and Domination.

The Ice Climbing Axe is the only new weapon in this drop. The battle pass gets a new Winter Offensive bonus path, just like we’ve seen with previous seasonal stages. This is how you unlock the axe, too.

Easily the most interesting change in this update is the range of improvements to audio across the board. First, footstep audio received a big pass that should make it easier to hear enemy footsteps, easier to locate them, and across different surfaces.

Some of the bugs that caused certain sounds to simply vanish have been fixed. This was especially prevalent in battle royale matches. BF Studios explained in the patch notes that it has adjusted memory priorities for in-game sounds in order to prioritise the most crucial ones. This is not the end of the road on audio, however, as the developer continues to work on making the soundscape more stable and reliable.

Some of those audio changes are the result of recent testing done in Battlefield Labs, which is also responsible for another exciting addition in this latest patch: improvements to hit registration.

While BF6 has had solid and stable netcode, certain situations would sometimes create uncertainty about how you died, and why certain actions seemingly failed to perform at that particular moment.

The focus in this update is to improve the reliability of how actions in close-quarter combat are translated, which includes firing before fully going into ADS, quick aim changes and more.

Speaking of close-range, the patch also brings another pass to soldier visibility to make it easier for enemies to stand out from the background. This is particularly relevant in areas with low contrast, or busy environments with lots of particle and visual effects.

1.1.3.0 also brings yet another set of weapon handling and gunplay tweaks, this time focusing on accuracy issues with first shots. You can also expect more tweaks to attachment behaviour with regards to recoil.

Something else worth highlighting is that vehicle gameplay is getting several smaller tweaks that have to do with how they interact with the world, how their HUDs behave and more. Finally, your settings should no longer be reset after applying an update. BF Studios says there are still some instances where that might happen, but the issue should be fixed for the majority of players.

You can read the full change log on the Battlefield blog.

#4305. 10 Legendary Shields You Should Have in Borderlands 4

Aden Carter is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2020. He specializes in lists and guides, with a focus on RPGs, horror games, survival horror, Soulslikes, cozy/sim games, and action-adventure titles. Before joining DualShockers, Aden contributed to GameRant, XDA, Gamepur, I

Legendary items are the prize you are searching for in Borderlands 4. They will help you complete your build, and carry you into the different levels of Mayhem Mode.

With over a year’s worth of content added to the game, there are plenty of legendary items, which means you need to start refining which ones are best for your characters. Once you have all your legendary weapons, including legendary assault rifles, you need to move on to legendary shields.

Shields will protect you, give you some additional buffs, and help you fight back against the swarms of psychos and Order Troops across Kairos. If you haven’t obtained them already, these shields are ones that you should definitely get.

One of the best shields from the base game of Borderlands 4 is the Super Soldier, as it literally enhances your abilities, turning you into someone who can run and shoot fast. It is almost like you took the super serum given to Captain America. There are plenty of references and easter eggs to find across Kairos, too.

The shield has the ability called Power Play, which gives you an overshield whenever the shield refills. This is great for procing abilities on weapons like the Ohm I got that get benefits from overshields.

Additionally, while your shield is full, it grants you 25% increased fire rate and 25% increased movement speed, which is amazing on characters like Rafa and Loveless who can amp up their movement speed. If you want to get this shield, you will need to farm Vile Lictor in Terminus Range.

There are some shields that will carry you far into the game, and then there are shields that are perfect starting shields that pack a punch, and are great for new characters. The Firewerks shield is perfect for any new character that you create.

This shield comes with the Bundled ability, which fires rockets at enemies each time you get a kill. These missiles deal fairly decent damage, making it easier to clear crowds of enemies quickly.

Of course, being a shield you want to get early, you would expect to be able to farm this weapon early in the game, which you can. You can get this shield from Spashzone in Riptide Grotto, which is near where you start the game. Some legendary farming locations are trickier to find than you may think.

A shield is meant to keep you safe from damage, and the Onion is all about that by offering you a means of negating damage for brief periods of time. Instead of a normal shield, this is an armor shield, meaning it has multiple segments.

The ability Shallot Shell makes it so you are immune to damage for a couple seconds after an armor segment breaks. Since this shield often has four segments, you have four times where you will be immune to damage before the shield is gone.

It is great for increasing your survivability, and is perfect for characters who are a bit squishy. You can obtain this shield by farming Sludgemaw at Watershed Gate.

How do Borderlands 4's new Vault Hunters stack up?

Do you want a shield that will cause some devastation each time it breaks and refills? Well, you might want to get your hands on the Extra Medium then, as it will cause some serious devastation.

This shield isn’t the most protective, with it sitting near the average when it comes to shield health. However, this is made up for by the ability Nucleosynthesis, which causes it to trigger a nova that deals major damage in the surrounding area each time it breaks or refills.

Of course, you need to let the shield completely refill before you can trigger the effect again, but it is great for getting out of sticky situations, and you can obtain this shield by farming the Vault Boss named Inceptus.

One of the biggest things that kills me in Borderlands 4 is self-damage. I blow myself up all the time with grenades and other types of splash damage. It is a serious issue. Luckily, the Honey Badger fixes this issue.

The Honey Badger shield has the Ferocity ability, which reduces self-damage dealt by 90%, meaning you can take a hit from a grenade and not get thrown into a fight for your life. It is the perfect shield for those who deal a lot of splash damage all around them with Torgue weapons.

Of course, if you don’t have this issue, you can skip over this shield, but it is worth it if you do. You can get the Honey Badger from Big Oil in the Bloodstained Hollow as part of the Vault of the Damned DLC. For more gear, check out the best DLC weapons.

There are some shields that have amazing abilities that boost your damage, but this damage buff comes at a cost. For the Protean Cell, this cost is the shield’s health. Luckily, it has a lot of health.

This shield has the Direct Current ability, which drains the shield over time, but grants you a bonus 40% shock damage. However, while this ability is active, you take direct damage, meaning the shield won’t protect you, so you need to be selective about when you use it.

Use this shield correctly, and you will rip through enemy health bars in seconds. Just don’t get carried away or it could mean the end of your character. You can get this shield from Fractis in Grindstone of the Worthy.

There are plenty of weapons in Borderlands 4 that have been added in DLC. Which ones of them are the best?

Every character can have some sort of status effect build, which makes the Exfoliatrix a great shield because it can be used efficiently by every character. You just need to be running a status effect build.

The ability of this shield is Exfoliatrix, which increases your status effect chance for six seconds each time an armor segment breaks. Additionally, whenever an enemy receives status effect damage, you recover a portion of the shield.

If you are constantly dealing status effect damage, you will be well protected by this shield, and you won’t need to worry about taking damage. You can get this shield by farming the Digi-Rifts on Providence Island in the FL4K and the Last Resort DLC.

An interesting ability that some shields have is that they can spawn kill drones that help you damage enemies. The Little Sister is one of these shields, and it does a great job taking down enemies.

It has the ability Sister, which grants you a kill drone whenever an armor segment breaks. This kill drone fights alongside you, mimicking the element of the gun you are using, and dealing 25% of the gun’s damage.

It is a perfect little partner to help you on the battlefield, and one that will continuously deal damage for you, helping you to wipe out groups of enemies. You can get this shield from Throne’s Experiments in Research Center B-0451. It can also be dropped from the chests at the end of the Takedown at the Hadron Abyss.

The Watts 4 Dinner shield is pretty similar to the Protean Cell shield, as they both grant you bonus shock damage. While the damage buff is less for this shield, it is a far better shield overall.

The Watts 4 Dinner shield has the ability Overshield Eater, which makes it so enemies have an 8% chance to drop an overshield when hit. Whenever you have an overshield active, you get a bonus 25% shock damage.

This is very easy to obtain, especially if you have skills on your character that grant overshield. Giving you a consistent 25% damage bonus is amazing, making this shield one of the best in the game. You can get this shield by farming Origo in the Vault of Origo.

Nova shields can be really strong, especially when they give you a damage buff and also release a nova. The Cindershelly is great because it does both of these things, making it easy to take down enemies.

This shield has the Glass ability, which makes it so you get a stack of resolve whenever the shield is damaged. Each stack of resolve grants you 2% damage reduction, and when full of stacks, this means you have a 50% damage reduction.

To top it off, when this shield breaks, it releases a nova that deals a set amount of damage, but this damage is increased by 25% for each stack of resolve you have, meaning you can do an insane amount of damage with the blast. You can get this shield from The Backhive in Dissected Plateau.

There are plenty of legendary assault rifles in Borderlands 4, and we will show you how to get them all.

#4302. Where Winds Meet December's calendar is full of new content, including a new region and the mobile launch you've been waiting for

You're probably nowhere near done with what's already in Where Winds Meet, but you better believe there's more on the way.

Where Winds Meet already has a staggering amount of content, but that’s not the end of what we can expect. Developer Everstone Studio just revealed a host of new additions coming to the game this month.

It’s clear that the developer is committed to the free-to-play action RPG, and the game’s recent success on Steam, and PlayStation has more than likely solidified the team’s plans for the future of the game.

On the official Where Winds Meet account on Twitter, the developer shared a brief roadmap of some of what we can expect over the course of December. The roadmap is split into the four weeks of the month, covering everything from smaller quests to more larger additions.

The first week started off a little light, with two new Jianghu Legacy Quests: Twelve Years of Feuds, and An Unholy Prophecy. Both quests are currently available in the game.

The biggest addition, of course, is the new Roarding Sands region, which becomes available the same day as the RPG’s global launch on mobile devices during the second week. Roarding Sands arrives December 11, along with a new campaign boss dubbed River Master.

Discover the Winds of December:🗺️New Region: Roaring Sands🌊New Bosses: River Master and Feng Ruzhi📱Global Mobile Launch: Dec 12 (UTC)🗡️New Hero's Realm, Sword Trial and more! pic.twitter.com/d12Ra9uXwb

We also expect a new boss, Feng Ruzhi, to be added to the game during the same week, as well as the arrival of the Velvet Shade Sect. Two limited-time activities kick off during the same week, too; The Fortune Beyond Parlor, and The Great Faceologist.

The third and fourth weeks of the month bring us the Scarlet Shock Sword Trial, as well as the new Blazing Gale Dance Hero’s Realm activity. Where Winds meet wraps it all up on December 30 with the Fireworks Festival.

#4301. Community: "I Think Of Her Every Time I Play It" - Your Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Memories

With the Switch 2 remake of the N64's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time fast approaching, we recently asked Nintendo Life readers to share their memories of the 1998 original.

Whether you were a Zelda veteran taking your first steps into a 3D Hyrule or this was your very first encounter with the series, this particular entry holds an extra special place in many a player's heart, having a profound effect and eliciting emotions that have stuck with us ever since.

So, for those looking to reminisce as we await the new version, as well as Ocarina newbies and younger gamers who, perhaps, are wondering what all the fuss is about, here's a selection of the messages you sent...

Thank you to everyone who took the time to share these moments. Some entries have been edited for brevity and clarity.

Ocarina of Time is what introduced me to one of my best and longest-time friends. I picked up a used copy in the 6th grade, and got stuck navigating the Lost Woods. I was talking to someone about it on the bus ride home from school, and my (now) friend overheard me, and immediately jumped over and gave me advice. After I thanked him the following day, he let me borrow his strategy guide in case I got stuck again. That experience and the long-term friendship it resulted in cements this as not just my favorite Zelda game, but one of my favorite games of all time. Broosh

I was still at college when Ocarina of Time came out in the UK, and I clearly remember playing it religiously on my N64 each afternoon or evening after lessons, over about a three week period. Ocarina totally dominated my life for that brief period, and I genuinely felt like I'd lost a friend when I finally finished the main quest - all these years later I can still recall the hollow feeling of not knowing what would fill the void it left! Still one of the most memorable adventures I've ever had. Tom Charnock

Fighting Dark Link for the first time triggered something in me, as a kid it opened my mind to question who Dark Link was. Was Link capable of being evil? Another core memory I have is the first time I ever beat Ganon I quickly rushed to the phone and dialed my best friend and excitedly told him what I just accomplished. We used to switch turns when it came to playing Single Player games. And who can forget the TITLE SCREEN. Arkay

Not sure why this one sticks out, but in the Shadow Temple, fighting two Stalfos on the ghost ship made me feel like a badass. I was 10 at the time, admittedly. Mattock1987

I do remember one funny occasion where, I turned the N64 to mess around a bit later at night, when I was not supposed to, and went to the title screen, I pressed some buttons and somehow deleted my father's save. I didn't even realize I did so, I just thought it was cool there was keyboard where I could insert my name. Once he went to play the next time, he grounded me for 1 month. It was the first time I was grounded as well. Brandon Silva

My older neighbor had OoT when it came out, and I would go to his house to watch him play. We'd sometimes take turns, until we got to the well dungeon! I remember thinking it was such a scary, grown-up game. I got my own copy when our local Blockbuster rental store closed, and was barely brave enough for the Shadow Temple then. I love the variety of ambiences in Hyrule, and I hope the remake can convey how scary the original could be! Jake

Countdown Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Dungeon Crawl #7 - Grave Expectations

In a collective save played by every kid at my after school babysitter, my only contributions were earning the cow in the horse race with Ingo and the golden scale in the fishing minigame, which taught me the value of learning to take on the weird tasks in any group project. Zach

Playing it when it first came out in 1998, the beginning area felt impressive in the early days of games in three dimensions. But when I left the Kokiri Forest and stepped out on to Hyrule Field, I set the controller down and just sat there in awe. My kid-brain couldn't comprehend how vast a video game could be, and it was beautiful to stare at as the sun slowly set. To this day, each time I replay OoT, I always take a moment to relive that sight. I'm looking forward to being stunned again. Adam Hollerud

My brother and I used to play Ocarina of Time together in the early 2000s. We browsed the early fansites, especially those that documented known glitches. Replicating these glitches ourselves was endlessly entertaining. This was the era when rumors ran rampant and the idea of finding the Triforce didn't seem so far-fetched. Does anyone remember "turning all the gossip stones blue?" The doctored photo of the "Temple of Light?" This game reminds me of my brother and of the unique online culture that surrounded it. Mike DeCou

When both my grandparents were still alive, I used to spend a lot of time at their house, an apartment in a 17th-century building. Going there was an adventure in itself: a big entrance door, three flights of old stone stairs, the smell of soot, and finally, the front door to their big apartment. It was December, and from the very first day, everything felt like a prelude to the long-awaited Christmas Eve. My sister, my cousins and I couldn’t wait to spend some time together. My cousin had a Nintendo 64. I still loved my SNES, but I also had a PlayStation and was really into PC gaming. And 1998 was the year of Ocarina of Time. He owned the game, and I distinctly remember how jealous I was, how I felt almost like a traitor for not owning a Nintendo 64, after being a Nintendo kid for so long. He pushed the cartridge into the console, switched it on, and my world stopped. All of a sudden, I forgot about Doom, Quake, Duke Nukem 3D and whatever else I was playing at the time. I was home. It was Zelda. Matteo Guarino

I was in first grade when we got Ocarina. My mom played it mostly, but I loved watching. One time in school, I was trying to draw the item subscreen (yeah...) and couldn't remember what was in a certain spot. My classmate who was watching and had no idea what it even was suggested "I think you should put a giraffe there". My other classmate slapped me in the face when I told him about the different temples, because "Only God could have those" (church and temple being the same word in Hungarian). Krisi

I played Ocarina of Time so many times that I gave myself a challenge: beat the game with only the 3 hearts you start with, and I did it! (I’ve pictures to prove it) Joseph R Casper

As a 53 year-old, I didn’t get into playing non-sports games until the mid 2000s. Up until then, I was only using my PS2 to play FIFA and Gran Turismo. But my brother who’s four years my junior? He had every Nintendo console. Including the N64. In January and February of 1999, we lost our mum and dad very suddenly. They were only 47 and 51 respectively and it hit us very hard. At the time, I was already married and had our first daughter, but I went to my mum’s place to see my brother every day and I vividly remember one day just sitting there watching him playing Ocarina of Time. It looked utterly incredible and that memory, no matter the brevity, was fundamental in me migrating to Nintendo and playing all the big, proper games. The Zelda’s, the Mario’s, the Metroid’s. That probably isn’t what you guys at NL are looking for here, but for me, just watching Ocarina was huge. It absolutely helped the both of us escape the pain of bereavement, even if only for an hour or two. And, to us, that was priceless. The_Pixel_King

In 7th grade, The Legend of Zelda OOT was my entire personality! We couldn’t afford it when it first released, but in 2001, my parents surprised us with it. I was obsessed! I carried that beautiful N64 instruction manual around like it was my Bible, to school and everywhere I went, studying every page. Some of my favorite memories were sitting with my mom, trying to solve puzzles together, getting stuck, and celebrating when we figured them out. Looking back, it wasn’t just a video game. It was pure magic, a piece of my childhood I’ll treasure forever. Giodannie Isabel de leon

I cried when Link left the Kokiri Forest with Saria standing alone on the bridge in the Lost Woods and again with Mido expressing remorse over how he treated Link before allowing me passage into the Forest Temple. I sobbed when Navi left Link in the Temple of Time. I also [remember] feeling tears of joy after finishing the game and seeing all the lives Link had interacted with throughout my entire journey. I also sobbed when I beat Majora’s Mask and Wind Waker and seeing all the people I had helped and bettered their lives in the process! VirtualVisage87

Sitting before the big TV in the playroom, my friend Maysen and I gazing up at a wide open field, enchanting music beckoning us away to the time of castles and kingdoms and brave knights. Navigating a tricky gated area in the field, feeling so smart. Exploring a quaint village (with a spooky-at-night graveyard). Sneaking about a castle courtyard. Finding a fun yellow mask, at last being allowed to pass the gatekeeper. Then it gets hard! Now, I sometimes revisit this land, experiencing again the faraway, magical places. Imagining my dear friend sitting beside me. Brian

This game is one of my favorite early memories with my mom. I started playing before I could read very well at all. My mom would sit with me and read the dialogue, stories, and signs to me. She would help me solve the puzzles when I was frustrated or didn’t understand some of the lore specific words that were being used. It is one of my absolute favorite memories of growing up and I think of her every time I play it or see the Triforce tattoo on my leg. Thank you Nintendo for all of these awesome memories. Joseph McKinnon

I was already a Zelda super-fan years previously, and when news started coming out for "Zelda 64" my friends and I followed that religiously. So when the OoT release was finally coming, we decided to have a launch party at my house. A couple of us saved and pre-ordered the game at the same EB Games to make sure we all got the gold carts. Immediately after school, Mom picked us up, brought us to get our copies and picked up pizza on the way home. When we all got to my place, starting up that game was awe inspiring. The music, the graphics, everything sucked into Hyrule and enthralled from the start. We all took turns playing while others chowed down on pizza and eventually my mom came out with a cake for us that she had decorated with the Triforce! We played till all hours of the night. It's a vivid and cherished gaming memory for me even 30 years later. David Hannah

I got the 3DS remake in 2019 (I was late) after hearing that it considered the greatest game of all time. I dabbled in the franchise before. I played BotW, and while I love that game, my nine year old brain was used to Mario platformers. OoT was a better introduction with its smaller world. Despite that, I sucked at the game. I loved what I played, it was so cinematic, but when I got stuck on a puzzle, I'd give up and wouldn't come back in months. Thus, I finally beat the game earlier this year. (Yay). The_Mario_Bro

My brother got a cool Christmas gift from the U.S.—an N64 and Ocarina of Time. Even though he wasn’t really into gaming, I totally got hooked! I kept getting stuck and even used the library’s internet to find tips. I skipped school a few times and picked up magazines to help out. I’m not sure exactly how long it took, but I’d guess about a month. Alejandro A

I got Ocarina when it was first released on N64. I had hit a roadblock at the Water Temple. After watching me fail repeatedly, my sister brought me and my game to her friend who showed me exactly what to do. The solution was so simple I was so mad at myself. Then I panicked as he kept playing, so I made up something “we forgot to do” and had to leave immediately. Needing help, the victory was bittersweet. Joshua Younis

I remember before the game came out, there was a hype website with a flash game that taught you the correct path through the lost woods. My friends were all amazed when I just ran through without any trouble. Justin V

I was always a gamer, and so I had made friends with the Best Buy associate. When Ocarina of Time was about to release I went to Best Buy every day in my car until he told me it was in stock, and standing by for release. The night before release I went, and he sold me a copy. Gold cartridge. The night before it came out. I got home at 9pm, my sophomore year of high school and I locked in. I stayed up all night. One of the first people to ever play the game. One of the best gaming memories of my life. Ed Tilden

We're around halfway through these golden recollections - turn the page for tales of young love, final battles, tears, realisations, Sharpies, and uncondonable launch-day activities that are surely past the statute of limitations...

#4300. Bill & Ted Sidescroller to Launch Backerkit Campaign in 2027

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

For the uninitiated, Bill & Ted’s Excellent Adventure was a 1989 sci-fi comedy starring Alex Winter and Keanu Reeves as the titular duo of teenage weirdos who get a chance to travel through time, meet famous historical figures, and make mild nuisances of themselves. It also co-starred my personal hero and one of the greatest comedians of all time, the late George Carlin, as their host in a time-traveling phone booth, Rufus.

The film, as well as its two sequels, remains one of the hallmarks of late 80s, early 90s pop culture, with any proclamation of “excellent” being a great way to make millennials spontaneously start air guitar-ing. Outside its films, the IP pops up in mildly odd places every now and then, including, apparently, a brand-new video game.

Spider-Man's video game adaptations are just as wild and varied as his comic book counterpart's adventures.

Indie developer Art of Play Interactive announced today that it’s developing a brand-new Bill & Ted game, Bill & Ted’s Excellent Adventure Arcade, a hybrid sidescrolling beat ‘em up and minigame collection based on the first film. This game is slated to be bankrolled by a Backerkit campaign, which is planned to launch in February 2027 with a handful of physical rewards available for early backers, as well as presently unannounced other swag like collectibles and apparel.

According to the game’s Backerkit and Steam pages, Bill & Ted’s Excellent Adventure Arcade is meant to be a playable version of the original film, starting with Rufus whisking the boys away into history in the time-traveling phone booth and running them through 15 levels as they try to meet famous folks for their history report. The game will feature audio from Alex Winter, Keanu Reeves, and George Carlin ripped directly from the film’s original recordings. It’s all original stuff, by the way; the Backerkit page stresses that this project will not use any generative AI whatsoever.

Bill & Ted’s Excellent Adventure Arcade is meant to be a playable version of the original film.

The actual game seems to switch off between side-scrolling beat ‘em up and assorted minigames. Bill and Ted travel through the time periods, getting into scuffles or running away from them, and when they encounter a famous historical figure, you play minigames to earn their trust and get them to come with you, such as battling Beethoven in a music duel or beating Napoleon in an ice cream-eating contest.

Sébastien Benard's action roguelike has resurfaced with a release window after several years of radio silence.

The game is meant to be played in local co-op, one character per player, though you can also play it solo and assume control over both Bill and Ted simultaneously. After beating the game’s main story, you’ll unlock arcade mode for faster playthroughs, as well as the individual mini-games for piecemeal enjoyment.

As you often see for these kinds of campaigns, and especially those for popular IPs from the 80s, the Backerkit campaign for Bill & Ted’s Excellent Adventure Arcade is planned to be accompanied by assorted physical rewards for those who get in on the ground floor.

To start, everyone who backs the campaign will receive a free Rufus Metallic Phone Booth card; those who reserve their pledge for $5 will receive additional Bill and Ted metallic cards, and everyone who backs in the first 48 hours will receive a fourth metallic card featuring the “historical dudes.” These four cards can be built together with the included top and bottom pieces to create your own little phone booth model. According to the Backerkit page, there will be additional incentives during the campaign proper, including exclusive merch, apparel, and other goodies.

The game is aiming for digital release on Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, and PC via Steam. Additionally, the game will have a limited physical release, with boxes for the Switch and PS5 versions, and even a physical CD-ROM for the PC version. There also seems to be a knock-off SNES cartridge in the works, though I’m assuming it’s just a prop and won’t actually run on a SNES.

Open-world games are the norm for AAA developers, but games funded on Kickstarter can deliver immersive open-worlds too.

#4299. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – October 23, 2026

This week has been home to some disheartening news. BioWare, the creators of games like Mass Effect and Dragon Age, is being shut down amid a flurry of layoffs. It's another frustrating story from a struggling video game industry. Below you will find some of our stories about the legendary developer, including our massive 2016 oral history. And then after that, you can read about our recommendations of what to play this weekend.

I spent the early hours playing Final Fantasy Resonance trying to figure out precisely why I couldn't put it down. I eventually realized that the game manages in a very purposeful way to answer that quiet need I've so frequently had: "I wish I could experience a game just like Final Fantasy IV or VI again, for the first time, but with a new cast and story." That's pretty much what you can expect here; Resonance is a very purposeful throwback experience that harkens to the early days of FF pixel adventures, but with several modern conveniences, graphical flourishes, and depth added into the mix. It's a big and refreshingly wholesome journey of entertaining party members, summoning giant creatures, flying an airship across the world, and fighting turn-based battles that include absurd spell effects. It's one of my favorite games of the year, and well worth the time it will take to explore. Read our full review for more.

Expect to hear a lot of people proclaiming this as "one of the good ones," as Modern Warfare came out swinging this week with a strong campaign, compelling additions to competitive multiplayer, and an impressive extraction shooter mode in the form of DMZ. I've already been impressed by the first few hours of the campaign, which offers a tense, harrowing, and often disturbingly brutal story that bounces between a number of character perspectives. The gunplay feels tuned in, the traversal and melee is satisfying, and the narrative beats grounded in excellent actin performances. Our reviewer has spent even more time with the full game, and can share their full perspective to help inform whether you want to take a dive into this year's installment.

The Nintendo Sports franchise, which began with Wii Sports in 2006, has never been about the single-player experience. That remains true 20 years later in Nintendo Switch Sports Resort. But this time around, Nintendo has boosted the amount of content beyond what the series has typically provided, appealing to all player counts, all while retaining its trademark approachability. Whether you're joining together with three friends for some friendly competition across the package's 12 sports or you're trying to climb the Island Crown ladder by beating increasingly difficult single-player opponents, Switch Sports Resort is a great motion-controlled collection.

Halloween is around the corner. As you’re buying overpriced candy, deciding which version of the Joker to dress up as, and debating between watching Obsession and Backrooms over a cup of cider, it’s the perfect time to replay old horror games or dive into new ones. 2026 has a solid roster of choices for the latter thanks to releases like Resident Evil Requiem, Paranormasight: The Mermaid’s Curse, and Silent Hill: Townfall, but Tenebris Somnia shouldn’t be overlooked if you’re looking for a cool indie throwback.

Part retro-inspired adventure game, part live-action indie horror film, you’ll uncover the mystery of a nightmare-induced apartment building and battle horrors to rescue your trapped ex. The gameplay is survival horror 101, but it’s executed well, with consistently clever and inventive puzzle-solving as a highlight. It may not be a graphical powerhouse, but Tenebris Somnia still maintains a creepy atmosphere thanks to solid scares partly delivered by effective and well-made live-action cinematics. If you’re going to binge horror films, you may as well play one too. You can read my full review here.

Full disclosure: I have not played One Piece: Grand Gourmet. I was trying to finish up Castlevania: Belmont's Curse when a review game landed in my lap that I've had to give my full attention. That said, I have watched a lot of the One Piece anime, have a cat named Nami, and dog named Luffy.

I don't know if One Piece: Grand Gourmet is any good, but I like the premise and pixel graphics. One Piece is a very malleable franchise (which is why its live action adaptation is pretty good), so the idea of managing a restaurant as Sanji feels like it could be a very good fit. I plan on climbing aboard with all my hopes and dreams soon. And it is out now, which is good to know.

Similar to the entry above, I have not yet played Stupid Never Dies yet (there are too many video games!), but we like to use this weekly article to call out the new video games of the week. I am eager to check out Stupid Never Dies primarily because of its pop-punk soundtrack and 2000s aesthetic. I think it has the potential to be a fun, nostalgic throwback to my youth when I was learning Blink-182's "Dammit" on guitar and playing Devil May Cry.

The Blood of Dawnwalker has been out for just over seven weeks now, but I wouldn't blame you if you haven't finished it – or even started it – yet. A lot has come out! But if you need a reason to jump back in, this week's 1.1 update is a great excuse – the devs have added hundreds of bug fixes and other minor improvements, so it should run better than it ever did before. There's also an even easier difficulty mode if you want to cruise through without worrying about combat, and a new in-game potion that lets you respec all your skill points. I stalled out about halfway through (when I started playing Wolverine), but I'm planning to jump back in this weekend.

Oh, and you can pet dogs and cats now. Maybe I should have led with that.

Multiplayer physics mountain-climbing game Peak became one of the most viral co-op experiences of 2025 (I refuse to use the term friendslop), but only PC players have enjoyed its wacky shenanigans. That changed this week as Peak is now available on PS5, Xbox Series X/S, and Switch 2. Either alone or, preferably, alongside up to three friends, you’ll try to ascend procedurally generated, absurdly unrealistic mountains riddled with dangers. Working together is key, a tricky prospect thanks to the in-game proximity chat that necessitates sticking together, but griefing each other, intentionally or otherwise, is just as entertaining – maddeningly frustrating at times, but entertaining. Peak on consoles includes all post-launch content and, best of all, supports crossplay for all platforms.

The original Azul remains one of my all-time favorite games even after many years, but it just misses the bar with its strategic complexity to be one I'd pull out to play with the kids. That why I was especially delighted to find that Azul Kids is one of those rare "adapted for children" projects that turned out extremely well.

Players take on the roll of creative young artists building mosaic displays with various colored tiles. The concept remains simple enough to work for even very young players of age five or six, but the whole family should have fun with the approachable strategy implications of choosing tiles and completing your masterpiece.

#4297. Battlefield 6's latest update dubbed the game's simultaneously best and worst patch as it runs into all kinds of issues

What's likely going to be the last major Battlefield 6 update of the year has launched with a number of unexpected issues.

There’s been a lot of anticipation for Battlefield 6’s version 1.1.3.0 patch. The patch kicks off the third and final phase of the game’s first season, adding some new holiday-themed content. More the new content itself, the update’s biggest additions are almost entirely gameplay-related.

Unfortunately, for as much as the changes in 1.1.3.0 have been well received, the launch has been marred by a series of technical issues, some of which are a little unusual.

Immediately after patch 1.1.3.0 went live, players on PC started reporting massive stutters that would occur every few seconds. The issue is especially pronounced in Redsec Battle Royale, but much deadlier in traditional multiplayer.

Battlefield Studios quickly acknowledged it, pointing out a workaround that appears to be working for players on Steam. According to those players, going offline on Steam’s friends menu has fixed stuttering for them.

The issue remains for other players on PC, however, and the developer said it’s working on a proper fix.

Perhaps the most disrupting problem the patch has caused is one that prevents players from being able to interact with the game’s menu. Tiles become unresponsive, or outright unselectable when you try to hover near them.

Ironically, the top set of tiles designed to make it easy for players to quickly jump into the new content has been the most affected. Restarting the game sometimes fixes the issue, and some players report that it only happens upon first launch after installing the update.

But Battlefield Studios later clarified that, unsurprisingly, there’s an actual reason behind the bug. Once again, a fix is being investigated, and the developer will offer an update once some progress has been made.

A little further down the list of importance is an issue that stops players from being able to skip tiers within the new Winter Offensive bonus path in the game’s battle pass. BF Studios took out the feature entirely while it works on a fix, so while you can continue making progress in the bonus path, you won’t be able to skip tiers.

This is all a shame to see. Outside of all the problems, the meat of the new update has been almost universally praised. The visibility improvements, and netcode updates have been celebrated. Many players were also happy to see meaningful updates to footstep audio and overall clarity.

It’s also unusual for a Battlefield 6 patch to run into so many issues at launch. The sentiment around 1.1.3.0 so far is that it’s the game’s best and worst update yet. Hopefully those issues will be fixed before the development team breaks for the holidays.

#4296. XBOX Confirms What Everyone Knew About The Elder Scrolls 6

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

Elder Scrolls 6 has been the talk of the town for months, with whispers of announcements and gameplay showcases constantly circulating. Bethesda has been resting on its laurels for quite a while now, using adaptations and remakes to buy time while they work on new entries in both of their flagship franchises.

Wuthering Waves is one of the biggest Gachas on the planet, and they do far better than most at answering player complaints. Let's go over exactly how!

Still partnered with and owned by XBOX, the title of Bethesda’s newest fantasy epic has been a bit of an open secret, one finally confirmed by the biggest names at XBOX. In a Twitter post, Asha Sharma herself announced the title of Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel. Continuing the theme of subtitles marking the game’s major locale, it’s easy to assume ES6 will take place in the capital of the same name.

Elder Scrolls 6 won’t be the first time series long players have entered the opulent city of Sentinel, as the desert-flanked capital also appeared in Elder Scrolls Online, and as far back as the original The Elder Scrolls: Arena.

Sentinel has a rich history for both players and the setting itself, standing apart as a city flanked by opposites, in both politics and environment. The split between ocean and desert does wonders to make it feel truly fantastical, while Bethesda has taken care to use real-world analogues to make the title location feel genuine.

After Skyrim’s focus on ice-cold mountains and Norse-themed culture, the Redguard housing Sentinel is set to be a major visual shift, one primed to breathe new life into the franchise. Bethesda is kind of playing with fire here, as many are expecting Sentinel to be an absolute blockbuster rivaling Skyrim’s universal acclaim.

With a new location to explore, one deeply ingrained in the lore and worldbuilding of The Elder Scrolls as a whole, Sentinel has the potential to be Bethesda’s biggest game ever, especially since the new Fallout is being handled by the team at Obsidian. With all their cards on the table, Bethesda are remaining remarkably tight-lipped, only unveiling the proper subtitle on their time, even when most already knew it.

There’s a respect to be paid for the adherence to their own schedule, but they’ll need to keep a tight ship. If Grand Theft Auto 6 has been any indication, there are individuals willing to hard focus on leaking major titles if the opportunity presents itself, and if proper gameplay or story spoilers manage to leak, I don’t think Bethesda will be able to stick their heads in the sand and wait it out.

For many, despite its age, Skyrim is still the archetypal fantasy RPG, a showcase of everything the general public wants out of the subgenre. Magic, monsters, and wild opportunities to help define both the setting and player character as an individual are all expectations they’ll need to meet, primed with experience and feedback from their latest attempts.

Elder Scrolls 6 won’t be the first time series long players have entered the opulent city of Sentinel, as the desert-flanked capital also appeared in Elder Scrolls Online, and as far back as the original The Elder Scrolls: Arena.

After the crash and burn of their most recent RPG attempt, Starfield, Bethesda needs to redeem themselves in the eyes of the general public, even as remasters like Oblivion and drops like Doom: The Dark Ages buy them time. It’s so exciting to think about one of the titans of the RPG genre returning to form, but it’s a little hard to be blindly optimistic.

Bethesda's hopes for the next generation are all riding off the back of Elder Scrolls Sentinel. Maybe a return to such an established region will give them the flow state they need to win back the gaming public while putting out their best work. The devil you know, after all.

#4295. Arc Raiders gets a few map exploit fixes in latest patch as Embark prepares to slow down how often patches are released

There's a new Arc Raiders patch that's fairly small, but one with fixes everyone is going to appreciate.

The time has arrived for another Arc Raiders update, and Embark has certainly delivered. Today’s patch, version 1.6.0, is among the smallest the game has received so far, focusing almost exclusively on disabling map exploits.

Perhaps more important than the patch itself, however, is the announcement the developer made around it.

Starting off with patch 1.6.0, it takes out a particular zipline on Stella Montis, the game’s most recent addition ot the map roster. Some players used said zipline to get out of bounds, something the game has been battling on several of its maps.

On Blue Gate, the patch fixes a collision issue that allowed players to vault through a wall, and fall to their death. The map fixes continue with another on Spaceport Launch Tower, which takes out a gap in collision that players have been able to shoot through.

The last change in this update affects gameplay feel around Arc enemies. Certain materials in the game’s world weren’t blocking their vision - or fire - when they should have, and this has now been fixed.

Alongside today’s patch, Embark also announced that going forward, we’re going to see fewer patches for Arc Raiders. The game has been getting updates almost every Thursday since it launched in late October.

Now that most of the major problems have been fixed, the studio is shifting to a slower patching cadence. Critical fixes will still be issued as soon as they’re developed, but don’t expect a patch each week going forward.

Embark also revealed that patch releases and in-game store rotations will now occur on Tuesdays. You should also expect the next few weeks to be quiet, as members of the team go on holiday breaks.

But, before everyone goes away, the game is going to get one more big update. The last item on Arc Raiders’ roadmap, revealed in early November, is the Cold Snap event. This is on track for Tuesday, bringing some new content alongside a few other fixes.

#4294. Phantom Blade Zero Review In Progress – Shaping Up To Be One Of The Best Action Games I've Ever Played

Phantom Blade Zero is an astounding achievement for the action genre. So astounding that I feel pulled to experience everything it has to offer… and that means instead of rolling credits, I’ve been busy completing story-critical side quests and more to get the most complete ending. That’s another way of saying I am enjoying this game very, very much but still need more time to render a final verdict, which is why you’re reading a review-in-progress of Phantom Blade Zero rather than a scored piece.

Though I’m not interested in guesstimating a score right now, I know it will be high because Phantom Blade Zero impresses and then some. It is one of the best action games I’ve ever played, and I’m shocked to be writing that. This is a debut of sorts for developer S-Game, which has dabbled in mobile games and smaller-scale titles; it’s the team’s first triple-A release, and its first game of this kind. This studio is so clearly a dedicated student of the genre, analyzing what works here and what works there in other action greats to create something of its own. It looks forward at what action games can do, can play like, can look like, while looking back at the games before it and understanding why those games – games like Devil May Cry, Elden Ring, Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, Bayonetta, and just about every other quality action game you can think of – continue to be ones we hold so highly. Should it stick the landing, Phantom Blade Zero will join that echelon of action pedigree.

Protagonist Soul is a quiet, mostly stoic martial arts master who prefers to let his blades (of which there are so, so many) do the talking. The Order he’s sworn his life to betrays him, and, in an effort to right wrongs, he discovers a villainous conspiracy to seize full power of the blood-soaked Chinese martial underground known as Wulin. As a result, puppets, secret sects, powerful god-like creatures, monstrous beasts, and much more prowl Wulin’s various biomes. I haven’t kept count, but there are a massive number of enemies to take down, both standard mob variants and bosses, and the game stays fresh throughout. It's even fresher when you consider how many weapons you can acquire on Soul’s journey.

Every weapon is wholly unique, like picking up a new character in a fighting game, each with its own moveset and abilities. Upgrading these weapons through various tiers unlocks additional abilities, and you can even Soul Temper weapons to add one final, game-changing ability or perk. A fully upgraded weapon can have a moveset that uses the majority of buttons on your controller. You can do the same with Phantom Edges, special tide-turning weapons with limited uses (before you build up additional charges). Combined with different accessories and medicine types, Phantom Blade Zero offers hundreds, perhaps thousands, of combat kit permutations. You can play as a drunken fighter who switches between sober, tipsy, and drunken states, with his range and damage output changing as a result; you can focus on a bleed build, ripping enemies to shreds with charged attacks that utilize Soul's own HP to deal extra damage (that can then be earned back with bleed); you can use lightning, wind, fire, and ice to create elemental storms against enemies, and you can use a sword that switches between different elemental states on command as well. You can also just pound enemies to pulp with Phantom Edge fists, too. I’ve struggled to stop using these fists since acquiring them because they’re so satisfying.

Forty-plus hours into Phantom Blade Zero, it feels like I’ve played as dozens of different Souls because I've discovered so many build types. S-Game smartly pushes you to try new builds and weapons as you get them, doling out generous upgrade materials and currency; it encourages you to try everything, and the next weapon might just become your new favorite.

Finding these materials (and additional fights) is great fun, too, because Phantom Blade Zero’s various open-area biomes are a genuine joy to explore. You are always rewarded for taking the optional path, and those rewards are always worthwhile. You might find a healthy pile of upgrade materials, or a boss with a weapon you’ll fall in love with. The way buildings, alleys, caves, cliffsides, and other environmental features weave in and out of each other evokes FromSoftware’s architectural design and the subsequent shortcut “aha!” moments.

That said, Phantom Blade Zero is definitively not a Soulslike, though you’d be forgiven for assuming as much given its challenging suite of bosses, interconnected world, and Phantom Bell checkpoints, which are this game’s equivalent of bonfires. However, its challenge is much more surmountable (with various difficulties and accessories to ease parry and dodge timing), and its world progression is materially different. Kill an enemy and it’s dead for good, which to my surprise, adds a sense of worldbuilding I didn’t know I wanted. Progression through this journey feels tangible because I’m actually removing traces of evil with my weapons, traces that don’t respawn when I interact with checkpoints. It’s a nice change of pace that narratively speaks to Soul’s efforts.

Along the way, countless reading materials shed light on Phantom Blade Zero’s intertwining stories, and tracking down the next memory, scroll, or book entry rewards you if you’re interested in the full picture of this Wuxia story. I’d argue the game’s story is its weakest element, but only when compared to the rest of the package. It doesn't break any new ground narratively, but it provides enough mystery and thrill to keep things moving. And while performances are great, talking to characters is still mostly just two people standing across from each other talking through a new quest. Fortunately, cutscenes pick up the slack with dramatic villains, heartfelt revelations, raw tension, and more.

Production value is high across the board, thanks to incredibly impressive animation and a beautiful rendering of this dark fantasy China. Faces are lifelike, nudging up just shy of the uncanny valley as close-ups reveal porous details, lip quivers, and more, bringing an excellent cast of Chinese performances to life. The English voice acting has its standouts, but Soul’s voice is boring, so I highly recommend the Chinese vocals.

Boss fights draw clear inspiration from Chinese cinema and boast a wondrous sense of awe and scale that only the best in the genre typically offer. There are a ton of bosses, too, with very few repeats (repeats do happen in segmented challenge trials), and it’s impressive to think back on just how many I defeated, and just how many of them delivered a unique fight. I appreciate the checkpoints between boss phases as well. There are so many bosses – nearing 100 or more if I had to guess – and having my progression saved through phases removes some of the repetition I often feel when, say, phase two of a boss continues to kill me and I have to blitz through phase one again and again before taking another stab at it.

That scale and on-screen excitement carry through almost every fight in the game, down to even the simplest mob fights, though these are starting to feel a touch repetitive as I’m barreling toward the game’s end. Soul moves like the world’s greatest martial artist, but your controller inputs make it happen. If you mash the attack button, it looks nice… but if you use each weapon’s prescribed inputs and abilities, Phantom Blade Zero delivers a level of detailed action I’ve seen in few other games. You direct the game’s action, and this lets you turn what might otherwise be just another group of fodder enemies into an electric bout of spectacle.

To say I greatly enjoy this game greatly undersells my feelings – writing this review-in-progress is frustrating because I want to get back to Phantom Blade Zero. I expect to reach credits in the coming days, so please be on the lookout for my final verdict this week.

#4292. Rockstar Moves Up GTA 6 Pre-Load Date, Confirming Massive File Size

Rockstar has brought Grand Theft Auto 6's pre-load date forward by two days and finally confirmed how much storage we'll need. According to a new Newswire announcement, pre-loading begins on November 10 instead of November 12, and the file could require up to 212 GB of space, depending on the device.

According to a new rumor, Rockstar Games could release the GTA 6 PC port just a few months after the highly anticipated console launch.

With the game still scheduled to launch on November 19, that gives you a little more time to get the download out of the way. The earlier start is welcome news for anyone with a slower internet connection, although finding enough free storage might be the bigger problem.

In its Newswire announcement, Rockstar says the pre-load file will require "up to 212 GB depending on your device." The developer also advises everyone to clear enough room before pre-loading begins. That's a substantial amount of storage, but the wording is worth paying attention to.

The phrase "up to" suggests that 212 GB is an upper limit rather than a fixed requirement for every console. Rockstar hasn't provided a platform-by-platform breakdown, and we still don't know whether the final installed game will take up exactly the same amount of space.

The figure is close to the 210 GB size reported on October 27 by PlayStation Game Size, an account that tracks information from the PlayStation Store. That earlier estimate concerned the PS5 version and wasn't an official confirmation from Rockstar. We now have a confirmed upper limit for pre-loading, although the final installation size remains unclear.

We now have a confirmed upper limit for pre-loading, although the final installation size remains unclear.

The distinction matters if you're trying to decide how many games to uninstall. The amount of storage required for pre-loading and the game's eventual installed footprint can differ, especially with updates around launch. For now, making at least 212 GB available, preferably with some extra room, seems like a sensible precaution.

I can already see this becoming a problem for me. My drives are usually left with just 10–20 GB of free space, mostly because I refuse to uninstall games I might suddenly get hyperfixated on again. I always tell myself I'll return to them someday, even if that means keeping them installed for months. If that sounds familiar, you might want to start clearing some space now.

Rockstar originally announced November 12 as the pre-load date, giving everyone a week to download the game before release. Its latest Newswire post moves that forward to November 10, with slightly different timings for each platform.

On PlayStation 5, digital pre-loading begins at midnight local time on November 10. Xbox Series X|S pre-loading, meanwhile, begins globally at 12 a.m. GMT on the same day. That gives console owners several days to finish downloading what could be one of the largest games in their libraries.

Rockstar's information hasn't been entirely consistent, however. Its online store listing still mentions November 12, while an older section of its customer support article also retains that date. The same support article now includes the updated November 10 timings further down, matching the latest Newswire announcement. For anyone planning their download, those newer instructions are the ones to follow.

The change also raises questions for anyone buying a physical copy. Rockstar previously confirmed that boxed editions of GTA 6 will contain a download code rather than a game disc, with retailers expected to begin distributing them on November 12. That schedule remains unchanged in the latest announcement, so anyone waiting for a boxed copy will still need to receive and redeem their code before downloading the game.

Pre-loading won't unlock GTA 6 early, of course. The game is still scheduled for November 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. But after years of waiting, having the download finished ahead of release is one less thing to worry about. I'd certainly rather spend launch day playing GTA 6 than staring at a progress bar.

South Park has aired real GTA 6 gameplay supplied by Rockstar, showing a crowded Vice City beach and Jason using a bag of dog poop to attack an NPC.

Sucker Punch, the team behind Ghost of Yōtei, Ghost of Tsushima, Infamous, and Sly Cooper, has been hit with layoffs, according to a report by Aftermath. The outlet states that 26 roles have been affected as the studio prepares its next project.

Aftermath cites a former Sucker Punch employee who confirmed the number of layoffs. The outlet also obtained a company email announcing the staff cuts.

“After carefully observing the challenges in the market and reviewing the team needs for our next project, we've decided to make some staffing reductions. #4287. 10 Pokémon Battles That Break the Rules of the Games

Laurence Wall is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been writing professionally since 2022 and covering games since 2023. He primarily writes guides and lists, with a focus on indie games, RPGs, ARPGs, Soulslikes, MMOs, card games, boss fights, and detailed tutorials. Before joining DualShockers, Laurence worked as

Pokémon games have never really been much of a challenge. I mean, that’s why Nuzlockes are so popular, right? You need to artificially inject some difficulty into the titles to really make the formula work.

However, while most trainers and Pokémon in the series follow the rules, others sometimes break them in one way or another. Intentionally or otherwise, this creates some of the more interesting challenges as the devs try to balance scales that are invariably tipped in our favour.

Let’s look at some of the most interesting examples, and why they make for such fascinating encounters.

This one is pretty famous, especially if you’ve ever Nuzlocked Ultra Sun and Moon! But why does this battle break the rules?

For starters, this battle is more like a trainer battle: you can’t run from this fight or catch Necrozma. No, it must be defeated! And if that wasn’t annoying enough, as soon as you enter the fight, Necrozma gains +1 to every stat.

On top of that, Necrozma has great coverage with its moveset and the ability Neuroforce, making its super-effective attacks even more potent. The thing is, you might have seen inherent stat boosts before, but they were from Totem battles! Necrozma isn’t even a totem Pokémon, and still gets a ridiculous amount of buffs. Getting through this battle without losing a single Pokémon is a massive challenge.

This list covers some of the best Pokémon ROM hacks to attempt a nuzlocke challenge.

I remember the first time I played Pokémon Yellow and ran into the Ghost. Honestly, the whole vibe of Lavender Town and the Pokémon Tower really freaked me out. But then again, I think I was like 4 or 5! Now this Ghost isn’t a Gastly; it isn’t even a Pokémon… not until you have the Silph Scope at least!

Of course, we all know it’s a grieving Marowak, but oddly enough, even though this really should be a regular Pokémon battle, you can’t catch this Marowak, no matter how hard you try. At least Necrozma gets an excuse; Marowak isn’t even legendary.

The thing is, though, in the original Generation 1 games, you can use a Poke Doll to escape the battle. If you do it this way, the battle is considered over, and you're the victor.

The Pokémon Mystery Dungeon series is pretty infamous for having ridiculously unfair battles that pit you and your partner against a massive number of opponents. Whether it's the entire cast of your Guild or Darkrai and 6 other Pokémon from the Dungeon surrounding you! But you always come out on top!

Well, one of the most annoying things that always seems to happen in these games is that your victory often means very little. For example, in the Grovyle fight at Crystal Lake, it doesn’t matter whether you win or lose; the story plays out as if you lost.

The same is true of the battle against Snover in Bidoof’s Special Episode. Even if you find a way to win, the game assumes you lost, so putting in extra effort and using items in these fights is pretty pointless.

Generation 5 is pretty famous for having Pokémon with stupidly high evolution levels. Whether it’s Mienfoo at level 50, Pawniard at level 52 or Larvesta at level 59. Of course, the most famous of these is Zweilous, the Pseudo-Legendary of the games, which evolves into Hydreigon at an eye-watering level 64.

The thing is, if you remember playing the original Black and White and facing off against Ghetsis at the end, you’ll remember he has a Hydreigon as his ace. And, for some magical reason, it's level 54. On the one hand, I get Game Freak wanting to give cool, powerful Pokémon to trainers and give us a challenge, but 10 whole levels under? Whatever happened to treating your Pokémon with love and respect?

Ah, and speaking of having underleveled Pokémon, we have another cheater in our midst. The thing is, Lance actually commits another assortment of sins alongside having illegal Pokémon.

Let’s ignore his 3 underleveled Dragonite for now, and take a look at his Generation 1 and 2 movesets. First, as part of the Elite 4, Lance has a Dragonite with Barrier, a move it cannot learn in that generation. He shoots himself in the foot a little with this, however, as the battle AI is coded to always use super-effective moves, even if they don’t actually do any damage. So he will always use Barrier against, let’s say, a Gengar, because of its poison typing.

And he commits another error in the next Johto titles, where he has an Aerodactyl with Rock Slide, another move that can’t be learned in Generation 2. Either Lance is a huge cheater, or maybe he just knows some secrets that we don't!

This list covers the hardest Elite Four members from Generations 1-9 of the Pokémon games.

While Generation 8 certainly wasn’t my favourite, it did have some odd yet memorable moments. One of these shows up when you fight Opal, the Fairy-type gym leader of Ballonlea.

This battle introduces some fairly bizarre mechanics, not found anywhere else in the series. As the battle goes on, Opal will ask you questions about herself. If you get them right, then great, you’ll get a nice little stat boost. But if you get them wrong, your Pokémon's stats will actually decrease. Yep, not from a move or an item, but a piece of trivia, mid-fight.

And the thing is, the last of these isn’t even true. You have to lie to Opal, saying she looks younger than she actually is, to get the final stat boost! Of course, this fight wasn’t actually difficult, but it’s still an odd event!

And speaking of Generation 8, we have another major cheater over here. You’ll meet Avery in your adventure through the Isle of Armour DLC for Pokémon Shield.

Avery considers himself a bit of a rival, and as such, he will do anything to win. In the 3rd trial, you’ll battle Avery again; however, in this match, he will set up Psychic Terrain before the fight even begins!

Psychic Terrain is a pretty strong move that boosts the power of all Psychic moves by 50%, and it usually takes a full turn to set up. Unless, of course, Avery had a Tapu Lele… which he doesn’t! He realises this is wrong afterwards and pays the price! Good riddance, eh?

If you have Pokémon Sword, instead of facing off against Avery, you’ll meet Klara, who fills a similar role, acting as your rival as you progress through the DLC.

Like the previous encounter, during the 3rd Trial, Klara will scatter a load of Toxic Spikes on the field before the battle even begins, which feels a bit more devious. And this isn’t just 1 layer of spikes, but 2, meaning that you’ll have the Toxic variant instead of the regular poison! Because Toxic Spikes doesn’t wear off like Psychic Terrain, you’ll need to Rapid Spin these away, or send out your own Poison-type to absorb the poison.

The funny thing about these cheaters is that I actually really like this added challenge in Pokémon games. Lately, the titles have become laughably easy, perhaps because we’re a little older. So having your opponents cheat and get extra turns certainly levels the playing field a little bit.

Pokémon Colosseum and XD are some of my favourite Pokémon games of all time. They brought so much personality to the Pokémon animations, and the world feels much more alive and dangerous than in other titles.

At the end of XD, you’ll face off against Greevil, and realise he actually gets 7 Pokémon instead of 6! First off, you’ll have to face the awesome Shadow Lugia, XD001. If you like, you can end this battle immediately with a Master Ball, but if you want to catch it with something more interesting, like a Premier Ball, it is a rough fight.

Once that’s done, Greevil will battle you directly with a full team of Shadow Pokémon. Oh, and did I mention Shadow Moves are super effective against every regular Pokémon type? And if all that wasn’t enough, he also has the 3 Legendary Birds! Yep, this guy's team is absolutely stacked! What a brilliant fight!

Of course, if you thought that 6v7 was brutal, Volo will totally rock your world. The first time I fought Volo, his team caught me totally off guard. I knew as soon as I saw the Spiritomb and heard that classic music track that this was going to feel like a fight against Cynthia.

Cynthia is famously one of the hardest battles in all of Pokémon, being the Champion of the Sinnoh region. Now imagine if she had a Giratina that emerged after she was defeated… and then you had to defeat that Giratina twice, once in its Altered Form, and once in its Origin Form, all without being able to revive or heal your team. Yep, this was a truly unfair 6v8 battle, and it was glorious.

This is what I meant earlier about trainers who cheat. They make for some of the coolest moments in the series. Why would the main villain let you walk all over them and still abide by the rules? They would try to defeat you by any means possible, right?

So having Volo with effectively 8 Pokémon, plus a Legendary, made for one of the craziest and coolest battles of all time. I’m not sure any other trainer will live up to the awesomeness of that final battle! We will have to wait and see!

#4286. Diablo 4's next expansion is bringing two new classes to the game, one of which you can play right now

Lord of Hatred may finally make good on the Mephisto arc of Diablo 4's campaign, which started in the original game and carried through Vessel of Hatred.

Very much when we expected it, Blizzard has officially revealed Diablo 4’s next major expansion at The Game Awards. Lord of Hatred delivers a new campaign that continues the mainline story, picking up from where Vessel of Hatred left off. Mephisto, the eponymous Lord of Hatred, has seemingly finally escaped imprisonment to rule over Sanctuary.

Lord of Hatred is the second Diablo 4 expansion, and it will be available on PC, PS5, Xbox One, and Xbox Series X/S on April 28.

It’s always a big deal when we get a new Diablo expansion, especially for a game as starved of fresh (major) content as Diablo 4 has been. But perhaps the biggest piece of news out of the Lord of Hatred reveal is that the expansion is bringing not one, but two new classes to the game.

The first of which is The Paladin, whereas the second is being kept under wraps. Even more surprising is that The Paladin is playable right now for anyone who pre-purchases the expansion. This is a well-timed shadow drop, especially given that Diablo 4’s latest season has just kicked off.

The expansion adds a new region to the world: Skovos, which is where the events of the new campaign will be taking place. This is the first time Skovos has been in a Diablo game. The region is of major significance to the world and lore of the series, as it is the birthplace of the firstborn, home of Lilith and Inaruis.

Lord of Hatred brings a decent number of major systems to Diablo 4. The endgame is getting a big overhaul, headlined by the new War Plans feature. Through this, you can effectively design your own endgame grind, creating challenges based on the activities you like and earning rewards along the way.

Endgame activities now also feature their own skill trees, which can be progressed through by creating War Plans for your character featuring each activity. The new endgame activity, Echoing Hatred, is something of horde mode where you must defend against unrelenting waves of enemies.

None of that matters without loot, of course, and the upcoming expansion is bringing back the Horadric Cube, and adding set bonuses using the Talisman system. The long-awaited and highly-requested Loot Filter is also coming to the game with the release of the expansion.

Beyond itemisation, each class’ skill tree will grow with new bonus skill variants. In fact, the entire skill system is being reworked for all classes - though details are a little sparse at the moment.

You can also expect the level cap to go up, which is very likely necessary to fit all the new skills and various systems. Blizzard offered a deep dive into the new Paladin class, which you see on the official blog.
